Urge urinary incontinence is leakage that follows a strong, sudden need to void that is difficult to delay. Many people experience a mix of both. Stress urinary incontinence is multifactorial. Pelvic floor muscle weakness is one contributor, but not the only one. Parity, hormonal changes, connective tissue laxity, hypermobility and altered neuromuscular timing all play a role. So I think the good news is there's a lot of optionality. The hard part is just figuring out which area am I going to try to build something? Am I going to hire consultants to come? Which type of consultants? Or am I going to be able to have an off the shelf product? So I think we're in a little bit of a confusion time for medium sized businesses, but also an exciting one because you can kind of itemize, pick apart your business and figure out what are all the areas that we can make more efficient? What are all of the areas that we can improve? So ultimately our customers, our end users, our stakeholders have a better experience. And the fact that the White House is supporting this, all the big tech companies are supporting this, I think is just moving everyone in the right direction. But it's not so clear, like the playbook isn't so clear. Right.

[SPEAKER_00]

We know a lot about Bill Gates. We know a lot about Mark Zuckerberg. We know a lot about Elon Musk. What about all these incredible builders who are, have built companies that have gone public or been acquired or just have making a real impact, but they're doing it in Brazil or they're doing it in Africa or they're doing it in the Philippines. And so I wanted to shine a light on some of these names, which are not necessarily household names for us in the U.S., but they are making an impact in their geography. So it's a fun read. It's a little bit travel journal. You'll hear my personal experiences traveling through all these countries, understanding the startup ecosystem. And then the interviews are really very personal with founders who have many of them come from war torn countries or from real developing ecosystems where it just hasn't been so easy to start a company. There was a lot of headwinds and they were able to persevere anyway with a lot of resilience really to chart their own path. And that is what the book is fundamentally about is how do we all develop and cultivate the entrepreneur within to chart our own path.

[SPEAKER_01]

[None]
Yeah.

[SPEAKER_00]

They've got a chip on their shoulder. They have something to prove and that they're not necessarily playing by the rules of politeness in a big company, but they're really have had to kind of, their ideas are so extreme that you have to kind of have that, that iron around you to protect you and that we should celebrate this. I think especially in America, it's not necessarily a characteristic that we like to celebrate, but honestly, this is what makes entrepreneurs great. This is what makes them persevere on big ideas. It's not because they're just talking about what everyone's talking about or trying to fit in. They really are the change makers out there. So that's one, that's a fun one for sure. I'd say the other thing that, and I go through kind of six of these principles, which you can read about in the book, but the other thing that was very poignant about doing these interviews, again, many of these founders have taken their companies public or their unicorns, their large, you know, somewhat successful companies at this point, as people were telling me their stories, because I always start at the beginning, your childhood, and

[None]

And as they recall and reflect on these experiences, it's very emotional. And that was something that was very unexpected because again, a lot of these founders have been super, super successful. One of them grew up in a small town in Pakistan and his family had never had, there was no education. He was the first person in his family. Meanwhile, he ends up building one of the largest or maybe the most successful startup in the Middle East. He ends up selling that to Uber for $3 billion. Right. And so I'm talking to him. And when you hear the vulnerability in their voice, or you hear them get choked up, you really realize that the founder journey for everyone is, is a really intense one.

[None]
Yeah,

[SPEAKER_01]
yeah. Founders are extremely interesting and unique individuals. A question from my side, just out of curiosity, how many of those founders and not from a purposeful choice through your own selection were female?

[SPEAKER_00]

So some great stories. One of my favorite ones is a woman named Lori, who's building just a massive company in Mexico. It's actually my first chapter. The company is called Kvac and it's a marketplace for used vehicles. And I don't know, the last valuation was $8 billion or something. And she's just epic. And so celebrating those stories, which we don't hear about as much, was really important to me.

[SPEAKER_01]
It's been fascinating. I want to thank you for your contribution today on Redefining AI. And I'm sure that our listeners will enjoy this conversation. Thank you, Jenny.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thanks so much, Lauren. It was a real pleasure.

[SPEAKER_00]

And so, as you can imagine, our portfolio is quite diverse. But we also feel that geography is becoming a lot less important in many ways, or maybe very important, however you look at it. But oftentimes we'll meet a founder and one founder will be in Austin and one will be in Indonesia and one will be in the UK. And it's like, well, where is that company base? So it might be a US C Corp, but the company is everywhere, right? Or is in different places? And their customer base might be diverse as well. So we believe, you know, we're pretty excited to be part of this kind of opening where geographies are becoming, you know, less important and we can really focus on what matters, which is really founders and founders finding interesting markets to sell into. So we're generalists. I think that our, what's interesting is that our deal flow, we're not, you know, outbound, we're not thesis driven, but our deal flow comes from our community of founders and operators who've all invested into us. fund.

[SPEAKER_00]
Techstars is the worldwide network that helps entrepreneurs succeed. What that means in practice is that we run close to 50 different accelerator programs. Each program is run by a different team in a different geography or market. The program I initially ran when I joined Techstars was our healthcare program in Los Angeles run in partnership with Cedars -Sinai, a large academic health innovator. Through that program we invested in roughly 40 startups at the intersection of digital health tech, medical devices, and providers. Consistent across all of Techstars in terms of what we're looking for as a firm is primarily an incredible, exceptional, passionate, coachable team. We believe that if you have an A -plus team, the product is less important. product can, know, an A -plus team will find the market, they'll pivot the product, they'll find the right people, they'll make the company work. Whereas if you have an A -plus product and a C -minus team, it's not a great recipe for success. COVID has sort of pulled back the curtain on how poor our adoption of digital tools and remote tools has been historically as a healthcare industry in the United States. And a lot of people are now scrambling to catch up and modernize and introduce basic experiences like text messaging your health system or telehealth. And so I've found this to be one of the silver linings of the epidemic, which is that I think the patient experience in the United States is going to be significantly improved as a result of providers and payers and med device companies and pharmaceutical companies all needing to find innovative ways to engage the patient and keep them healthy.

Hello, my name is Simon, I'm CEO and co -founder of Pimlock. So we're not an advertising company, we're never going to monetize your data. We want to give you the latest tools to enjoy and manage your image and video collections without you having to relinquish control. Everybody's image collections are full of very dense and very descriptive private data and most people, I assume most people in this room don't really know what's in their image collections. Most people don't have the time nor the inclination to go through every image and watch every video but as you've seen here in the last two days the machine can now do that very quickly and it's not a big step for these companies that you're providing your images into to start providing that data to insurers, potential employers as well as harassing you with more annoying advertising and actually whoops and if like me you enjoy a occasional drink that's probably something you're not necessarily going to want everybody to know. The other thing about personal image collections is actually a bit of a goldmine for someone that wants to hack in and get some of your private data. So one very quick search on my last ten years worth of images, which is about 30,000 images for receipt. I got about 700 responses, I found pictures of six different people's passports, medical records, share certificates, bank cards, my Wi -Fi password, lots of things my wife would never want anyone to see and I genuinely didn't know I had any of those things stored. You know with the usage of smartphones for documenting and the fact these things then disappear quickly into cloud storage systems actually there's a huge amount of data set in people's image collections but they just don't think about. So we've created a solution, it's Google Photos in a private box. It sits at the edge of your network in your living room, not somebody else's. You bring it home, you can connect it to your local Wi -Fi network via the smartphone app, the box is going to find all your images and videos, it's going to index them and then very quickly from the comfort of your home you can start to enjoy your past memories and your images and videos without having to give control of those away to anybody. The box ships with over 300,000 pre -trained classifiers so you can find the people, the objects, the activities, the locations and the scenes that you want to but alongside that basic functionality we've also built in some more advanced features for people with more specialist data sets, so keen hobbyists and people. So you can go and you can create new classifiers, you can improve them and we also have some new navigation tools for navigating much larger sections of images based on swiping and tapping on the content within them. tap an image of my wife's face and we'll give you all the images of my wife. And actually the edge -based processing and storage market is seeing a major resurgence at the moment. Analysts are predicting a 24 % growth over the next five years and we certainly think Pimlock's in a very good position to take a good slice of that. So we have projections to bring a range of products to market through direct sales but also some white label licensing of our platform. So the first thing we're going to do is we're going to launch our new box in August. We have two versions. We have a small memory version for people that already have adequate storage at home and a larger memory version for those that don't. You'll be pleased to know the platform already works, the electronics and the PCBs already done. We've had functional prototypes working for six months in a rail of trial areas. So all we need to do now is look for manufacturing partners for ramp up and pressing go on the tooling. We raised our seed round last October. We're currently starting to have conversations around looking for series A to take us through ramp up and initial batch production. And we've got a very special and fantastic team. So we've got two of the leading academics from Oxford University on the AI side. We have Julian who's set up and run actually three different computer vision companies in London over the last 30 years. We have James who built the original Hawkeye ball tracking system. That happens to be a bit of a genius. And then myself who's got a range of experience from Nokia and connected camera space recently. So thank you.

And most of my experience has been on the go to market marketing side. So it's certainly as you see an area we're going to have to build out as we start to see more pre -order sales come through. have all my stuff in the cloud. Or, you know, I don't want to have to worry about setting this thing up. Or if my internet's going to work all the time. Or if I can get my stuff from halfway around the world when I want to show somebody when I'm on vacation. You know, it seems like

of that obviously the expense and the complexity. So how do you think about that?

[SPEAKER_05]
So I'll say the first market we're going to go after is people that have yet to migrate their collections to the cloud.

[None]

the right customer, though?

To start with, I think that's a good place to start. I think there's going to be an inflection point happen. So far people have been used to sharing discrete curated bits of content with social networks and cloud providers. They've picked the item. They've shown it in a known way to a range of people. I think people are now only starting to understand the implications of here's 20 years worth of data on my life. And actually no one's really started to unravel that and understand, you know, what implications it has later on. So I think that will change. But I don't think we're there yet, is my point on that one.

We're the oldest IP Bar Association in the United States. We have over 800 active members, 25 standing committees. If you're not a member of IPLAC, we encourage you to join to not only come to exciting events like this, but those that we have throughout the year. So I'd like to start by saying thank you to Chicago Kent for offering this space. It looks like we've got a really nice turnout, so we're certainly making use of it. Personally, I'm really happy to have this event here. I have a lot of ties to Chicago Kent. Not only did I graduate here, but I have two siblings, an uncle and a grandfather, who all graduated from here as well. So we've got five total in my family. I'm also an adjunct professor here. I teach a class called Strategy as an Intellectual Property, so I still get to spend quite a bit of time at the school. I'd also like to say thank you to everybody who helped plan this event. We had a lot of people who put in a lot of time and effort, including Billy Hinnon, other members of the IPLAC corporate committee, a number of partners at MBHB, along with people at the director's office and here at Chicago Kent. So thanks to everybody across the board. So with that, I'd like to introduce our two guests this morning. The first, sitting closest to me, is Grant Druchess, managing partner of MBHB, who will be hosting today's fireside chat with our second guest, who I'll be introducing in just a moment. In that role, he was also involved in all other aspects of intellectual property practice, including prosecution, due diligence, and licensing. He's represented a number of clients across the technology spectrum, including those associated with medical devices, genetic testing, the internet, television broadcasting, video game systems, and computer peripherals, just to name a few. But, they deal specifically with the same petitioner filing another petition at some point after the original petition. Perhaps after they see the institution decision. Maybe the institution decision denies institution like in the example I just gave you. And, there's still time for the petitioner. The 12 months haven't expired. There's still time for them to file. Those factors do deal with that issue. And, to a large extent, we have significantly cut down on follow -on petitions by the same petitioner. You really have to have a good reason to have a follow -on petition and on the same patent by the same petitioner. There are other issues though. What about other petitioners? Right? Obviously, if it's a petitioner in privity with you and you're working together, maybe the same analysis applies. But, what if you're not in privity? Maybe, what if you're co -defendants in a case but not really working together? Or, there are parallel cases and you're not in the same case at all? Or, maybe the second petitioner is not even sued yet and for whatever reason they want to file a petition at some point. All sorts of questions like that. So, we are working through that as well. And, you will have already, you've seen a couple of decisions that touches on some of these issues. And, it could be that we would deny institution on a follow -on petition by another petitioner depending on a variety of factors. There is also a separate question about the same petitioner filing multiple petitions at the same time. I'm sure many people experience that here. For, you know, we have page limits or word count limits, whatever. And, some people think that they need to file multiple petitions, multiple bases for invalidity and the like. At some point though, you have to ask, how many petitions suffice on the same patent at the same time? You know, if you don't like your first, second or third ground of invalidity, for example, and you have to be into your seventh or eighth ground of invalidity, I mean, you know, why is it in the interest of the United States to devote so much resources to address every single ground for invalidity? Some district courts, for example, make you pick your best, ten best claims, for example, and things like that. There are other limits that we can impose on a discretionary basis. We are looking at that issue as well. And, we might have something on that particular question as well. Bottom line is, we want to give everybody a fair opportunity to be heard. But, at the same time, we want to avoid multiple bites of the apple. We want to avoid overburdening the system as well.

[SPEAKER_00]
Hey friends, thanks for joining me, Jim Baroud, to hear a few insights from leaders who represent our innovation ecosystem. Today's chat is with Jenny Fielding, the co -founder and managing partner at Everywhere Ventures and the author of the new book, Venture Everywhere.

[SPEAKER_01]
I'm a venture capitalist, and what that means is I invest in startups at the earliest stage of their journey. So just as they're getting going, sometimes even idea stage, we bet on founders, on their ideas, and on their potential. And previously I was an entrepreneur, so I've walked in those shoes and kind of taken a lot of the learnings, especially the hard ones, and parlayed it into my own style of investing in companies.

[SPEAKER_00]
Awesome. I look forward to hearing that story. Again, you're one of the preeminent investors and one of the, unfortunately, still a handful of, you know, a small amount of female investors in this space, but you're one of the OGs, obviously. And so delighted to have you talk about that a bit, but let's talk about that. mean, how does one go from high school, college to become a, you know, an investor? So take us through that journey.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, well, like to say I'm both an accidental entrepreneur and an accidental investor, and that seems to be the through line of my life is kind of stumbling into things, but not really seeking them. So started much more traditional. So I grew up in New York City. I ended up in law school. I worked in finance, kind of like took a very different path. And then one day I had an idea, not for a startup, actually, like, because that kind of terminology at the time wasn't even in my head. Like, most of my friends were bankers and consultants, and I just, like, didn't come from that, you know, that kind of tech ecosystem that really just didn't exist in New York at the time. But I had a problem that I wanted to solve. And like most entrepreneurs that I call empath entrepreneurs, right, so they're solving for their self, I was just trying to, you know, figure this thing out for myself. Well, that kind of turned into getting co -founders, turned into starting a company in my living room and growing that company to more than 100 people, running it for a number of years and having an exit. So very accidental, again, didn't start out seeking to be an entrepreneur, but just saw something in the world, as many entrepreneurs do, that just didn't sit right. And I wanted to find a solution for that. So that was how I started. I think once I got the, not just entrepreneurial, but kind of the tech bug, I knew I was never going back to kind of traditional, you know, law, finance, all that kind of stuff. Like it was just in my blood and I was so excited just about, you know, how you can make an impact in the future. And so I started another company and unfortunately that one was not as successful. But I actually think, you know, looking back, I probably learned a lot more from that second one. I learned a lot from the first one because I'd made a lot of mistakes, but, you know, my biggest attribute I think was timing. And as many entrepreneurs know, a lot of things are out of your control and, you know, market tailwinds, oftentimes, you know, you have nothing to do with them. But we got pretty lucky the first time. I'd say those tailwinds turned into headwinds for our second company, which was actually a really good idea. And I've seen many companies go on to great success kind of, you know, around a similar space. was a text message marketing company. But at the time in 2010, you know, many of your younger listeners won't even be able to relate, but I think you will. It was a little bit like offensive to get marketing on your phone. Your phone was this like very personal thing where you called your mother. And it really wasn't, you know, the supercomputer that we all have that we're glued to where we can do anything. And many people like honestly run their whole businesses on their phone, right? It really just wasn't that. And unfortunately, it was just a timing issue. Like we had a lot of good things. We had a lot of great team members. We had, you know, good backers. We had a lot of good, you know, got a product roadmap. But we just couldn't get people to kind of get over that psychology of it being intrusive. Well, now, I

[None]
mean,

[SPEAKER_01]
like what people get on their phones, like can't even, you know, can't even talk about. So, you know, that's just an example of being at the wrong side of a trend or, you know, just, you know, too early.

[None]
Well, let's go back.

[SPEAKER_00]
Jane, let's go back to the first company. What was that?

[None]
That was. Yeah.

[SPEAKER_01]
So the story is I had a boyfriend in Germany. I was making lots of international phone calls. And my mobile phone bill was about $1,000 a month. So very different than, you know, now calling again. Different time, 2007. And I looked around. I was working at J.P. Morgan at the time. And there were all these bankers that were actually not from the U.S. And they were calling friends and family. And they were using these, like, calling cards. I mean, these are people working at J.P. Morgan. And, like, they were also, like, going down to the little bodegas and getting their little calling cards. So I just thought, wow, like, there's a few different use cases here. And yet the technology is just so antiquated. And so, you know, could we create something to automate essentially what a calling card would do through an application on your phone? The iPhone had just launched. And all of a sudden, you know, we could do a lot more on our mobile devices. So, again, started out solving a personal problem I had calling the boyfriend and turned into, you know, a really kind of impactful company. Because now people, instead of, you know, paying, you know, hundreds of dollars a month to call their loved ones back in countries that they came from, they could literally do that for a few dollars. And so that was just this, like, kind of incredible moment where you could, like, really help people, you know, change their daily experience.

[SPEAKER_00]
That's great. Thank you for clarifying. That's really interesting. All right. So bring us back to where you saw the second one, second company, not so great. Then what did

[None]
you do?

[SPEAKER_01]
to shut it down. I was working on my third company and, you know, somehow ended up on the other side. So, you know, I thought I was going to take some time off. I was going to go on some big travels. But I ended up, you know, at a venture fund called Techstars. And when I met the founders of Techstars, they had thought, they said, you know, do you ever thought about kind of being on the other side and investing? Which I had. But I was really kind of thinking about my next company. And they said, yeah, come spend a year or with us. And I think you'll learn the other side. And I think what I really loved about that platform is it wasn't just about cash. It was really about community and resources. And that was the thing that was most lacking in my entrepreneurial, you know, journey. Because, again, I came from New York City, not Silicon Valley. There weren't co -working spaces. There wasn't venture capitalists. There weren't meetups. mean, there was just, like, nothing going on. And everyone said, if you're going to build a software company, you need to go out west. But I kind of looked around and I said, like, that doesn't exactly make sense to me. Because if you look at all of the pieces that we had in New York, it seemed like a great place to build a company. There wasn't that community. But, I mean, we had capital. We didn't have venture capital. But we had, you know, lots of rich people, Wall Street, you know, real estate people. So it's like, you know, there was a lot of money sloshing around. We have every multinational here that you could sell to or partner with. Incredible engineering schools where great talent was coming out. I mean, you know, New York had so much to offer. And yet people were saying you had to go to California. And I thought, that's, like, really weird. So I was definitely one of the earlier people building companies here. And, you know, it was really fun back then. It was a small community. And it was just, you know, kind of the beginning.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. And so I remember that. Oh, God. Through the years, just going into the city. was so exciting. I remember meeting Marissa Meyer at some meetup.

[None]
It

was just one distant memory. But early days. So then you went from Techstars to what?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So the other kind of through line in my journey is that I tend to kind of bootstrap things. So while I, you know, bootstrapped my first company, was working at J.P. Morgan and started that company nights and weekends, I did the same thing with my fund. So I was working at Techstars, kind of came up with the thesis for everywhere based on my entrepreneurial journeys, coupled with, you know, many years working with entrepreneurs, you know, through the accelerator model. hmm,

maybe I could come up with some type of hybrid where, you know, we had a lot of the kind of community and ethos of maybe an angel group. [None]
Got it.

[None]
Yeah,

so we invest at the pre -seed, which we define as small rounds, typically about 500K to 2 million. So not the Silicon Valley, like I'm raising a $10 million pre -seed. What we like to say is that we invest in what we call the resilience economy. Got it. And what, since you're all around the world, well, first of all, you have 500 LPs. Do they think they have sort of preferences if they send you deal flow? Or do you sort of lay down the law and say, it's going through the system?

And I really wrote this book for all the entrepreneurs, aspiring entrepreneurs and people that just want to live their life differently. So I hope that people enjoy it.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. And I'm sure I'll enjoy it because I'm going to buy it for sure. I love, love, love that you have put all these stories in a book and for anybody out there that's listening, I think it's, it's really worth just, just purchasing and reading this book. I'm sure you'll get a lot of good insight into startups and entrepreneur and, and everything else that you are, you've covered in that book. So thank you again and stay warm. And I'm sure that hopefully we'll cross paths and I will definitely read your book.

[SPEAKER_00]
Thanks so much, Veronica. It was really fun.

Thank

you.

Thank you.

[SPEAKER_00]
Hi everyone, this is Roch from Dyson Mossery and I'm excited to have Jenny Fielding, who's one of the most active global pre -seed investors. And she's the co -founder and managing partner of Everywhere Ventures. She's also the author of the new book, Venture Everywhere. Welcome to the show, Jenny.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thanks so much for having me. Excited to chat.

[SPEAKER_00]
Awesome. So, you know, you've been very active on Twitter. I've been following you for quite some time. But how did you get your start in the venture capital world?

[SPEAKER_01]
I feel like everyone now, you know, talks about my punchy Twitter. But I actually started, you know, a very traditional path. So I live in New York City. I went to law school. I worked at J.P. Morgan. So I was taking a very, let's call it, traditional New York corporate path. And then a long time ago at this point, in 2008, I came up with an idea for a startup. And I didn't even really call it a startup, honestly. I just had a problem that I personally, you know, saw an annoyance in the world that I wanted to be solved. And it was in the mobile telecommunications space. So I set up with some co -founders in my apartment, as many folks do, and bootstrapped this company. At some point, we actually had revenue. And everyone said, Jenny, I think you're going to need to leave your job. I

[None]
was like,

[SPEAKER_01]
oh, okay. So, you know, as you can imagine, 2008, there just wasn't, you know, much capital available. There certainly wasn't venture capital. So we had to be very scrappy. We had to bootstrap. And, you know, we just couldn't expect other people to bankroll us. So that

[None]
was where it all

[SPEAKER_01]
started. Started as a founder. Went on to found another company. And then ended up on the other side, to the dark side. First as an investor at Techstars. So in New York, running Techstars New York and some of the vertical programs. And now at everywhere.

[SPEAKER_00]
Interesting. And, you know, you started two mobile software companies, you know. So were you able to get an exit out of those companies that you launched?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. First one, I got very lucky. So, you know, there's a lot of hard work in running startups. But there's a lot of luck in terms of timing. And so we can never forget that as both investors and founders. So in my first one, you can imagine, the iPhone launched, I think, in 2007. So anything around mobile technology was super exciting, was hot. And if you happened to be building in it, you got a lot of attention. So I like to say, although we worked really hard and I think the idea was quite good, we benefited from the zeitgeist of everyone being super excited that all of a sudden you had this supercomputer in your pocket and all the things that you could do with it. My second company, I did not get as lucky, although I still think it's a great idea. It was a text message marketing company. And unfortunately, at that time, 2009, 2010, people, at least in the U.S., weren't really ready to get marketing on their phone.

[None]
Their phone still

[SPEAKER_01]
felt like a personal place where you called your mom and you got important information. And unfortunately, we had to shut down because we couldn't find product market fit. The irony, of course, being that we've seen many companies go on to huge success in the text message marketing space, and it was just a little bit ahead of its time. So I always think that that's what keeps you humble as both an investor and a founder is that it's not just about, you know, great ideas and new ideas and kind of seeing the future. But if you're too far ahead, that can also backfire. So those were some of my experiences, both with a good exit and good market timing and one that didn't work out so well.

[SPEAKER_00]
It's interesting, you know, because I'm Indian and I've seen a lot of companies back in India would promote on WhatsApp, but that's something which is not done here in the U.K. or in the U.S. I hope they don't bombard the messages across this platform. But, you know, you've been an operator and a founder. Why did you go on to become a VC? Why not, you know, build more companies since you've already done two weeks, twice?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, I mean, I was actually working on my third company when I came across the folks at Techstars who ended up, you know, hiring me and basically convincing me that learning about the other side, about venture capital, could be, you know, could be a great addition to my toolkit. Whether I was a founder or an investor, learning about the other side was really important. And honestly, I learned something about myself, which was I was a pretty okay founder. I had a lot of quirks and a lot of things I did wrong. But I was actually a really good kind of zero to one investor. So not just

[None]
about

[SPEAKER_01]
the investment part, but really about sniffing out interesting people, trying to understand what makes them tick, and ultimately, like a pretty good picker. So in my early days, you know, I ended up backing a few companies that went on to become unicorns and are still dominant players in the market. And so what I realized about myself was, you know, sometimes for your, you know, when you're building a company, you can't see what's right in front of you. You need someone to help you. And that, honestly, I was, like, really good at helping people see what they potentially couldn't see themselves. And that was kind of my superpower. And so at that super early stage, just surrounding founders with, you know, the knowledge, the resources, the support was really critical. It something I didn't have when I was starting my companies because it was a kind of different time. But that was something that I could bring to the table. And I was pretty good at it.

[SPEAKER_00]
Interesting. Yeah, I've had Brad Feld who have come on the board. I'm a big fan of Brad. But how has been your experience with Techstars? Is it very similar to what you get at Y Combinator or Firmware Startups? You know, it's one of the top three accelerators in the world. But how was your experience running Techstars?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, I mean, it was magical for me. It was kind of the early days. So I joined in about 2014. The company was still rather small. I think, you know, there was a handful of programs. And I think there was only 25 people full time when I joined Techstars. So it felt like a startup in and of itself. And it felt like we were doing something different. Which was not necessarily backing founders in the Valley who kind of had a lot of access already. But looking at founders everywhere else and how we could support them. So, yeah, it was a critical time for me. I think I learned, you know, a ton not just about investing but about, you know, building your top of the funnel. And how that community could actually help your portfolio and ultimately support your portfolio. So I definitely learned a lot through not just a traditional investing fund but through this really innovative accelerator model. Which now I think people are pretty familiar with. But, you know, back then it was a different model.

[SPEAKER_00]
Interesting. And did you want to venture out and create your own fund? How did the, you know, how do you think about, you know, building everywhere venture and building this community for founders and investors?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So the first thing I'll say is that when you build a micro fund, it is much more similar to building a startup than it is to, you know, becoming a investing partner at a large VC fund. So the number of hats that I wear in every day is the number of different things I need to do, different stakeholders. It feels much more like being a CEO of a startup. And I

[None]
actually like that.

[SPEAKER_01]
I think the diversity of what my day looks like, whether it is, you know, brand and

[None]
going on podcasts

[SPEAKER_01]
and expanding, you know, our name out there. Whether it is working with founders in our portfolio, finding new founders, or, you know, raising money from LPs. Like that is all part of the job. Not to mention that we have a team we need to manage. So you get to do a lot of different things. So, you know, the job is pretty unique. And that is the part I really like about it is the diversity of what you get to do. So that is kind of, you know, the, like, I love to say that to people because they always like, what was the shift from going from a founder to an investor spinning out? And I am like, honestly, all these things, the common thread is really starting something new and, you know, creating your own path. And that is honestly what the book is about as well, which we will get to.

[None]
But it is

[SPEAKER_01]
about, you know, not going after the conventional job or path and, you know, charting your own course. So the decision to kind of spin out and do my own fund was very organic. I saw, you know, something that I felt like was missing in the market. And especially in New York City where I felt like there was, you know, all these great founders. There were all these, like, now second time founders. And there wasn't really a mechanism for connecting them. So our first two funds, I was actually still working full time. And we started them kind of as proof of concepts, right, to

[None]
prove

[SPEAKER_01]
the thesis. Could we create something called community powered venture capital where our LPs, our backers, were other founders and operators? And I think, you know, this had probably been, you know, tried in a few other ways. But we were definitely one of the first to kind of come out full force saying that found other founders make great investors. founders founders are great top of the funnel deal flow. And ultimately, founders give good advice. So if we can kind of, you know, marry that trifecta, we would have something special. I think now you hear more people doing it, operator networks, et cetera.

[None]
But when we

[SPEAKER_01]
conceived this in 2017, it was definitely more unique.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And, you know, I've been an operator in TechStarter, but I had a question for you. Should founders who run, who, you know, it's At least series and above. Should they run their own syndicate or should they run their own fund or should they be like an LP in a fund?

[SPEAKER_01]
That's a hard question to answer. I'd say it's probably a mix.

[None]
So if

[SPEAKER_01]
you're someone that is, you know, really excited about the fund process, which again is not just about investing. It's about managing other people's money, which has a lot of components. And you have the time and acumen, then I think, you know, by all means running a syndicate or your own fund can make sense. I'd say most of the founders that I know are pretty busy being founders. They're grinding really hard and for them being an LP makes a lot of sense. I'd say one of the draws for that community to everywhere is that they really get to be along for the ride. So this is something pretty unique is we don't make a big distinction in our portfolio between who are portfolio founders and who are founder LPs. We really provide the same kind of access and community for them. So we have a Slack channel with all of those people. So we have 500 founder LPs and another 500 portfolio companies and everyone is kind of mixing, supporting each other, say in our Slack channel, has access to our CRM and kind of the suite of collaborative tools that we've built. They're welcome to come to all of our events. And so mixing that community, I think, is what's really interesting. And the overlap, as you can imagine, we have a lot of LPs that now have become portfolio founders. So, again, it's kind of taking it out of those clear boxes and saying, you know, there's a lot of mix between these communities. So why don't we just build a premier founder community and not worry about what label we put on them?

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And, you know, you focused on precedency and, you know, I've seen the last 10 years, there's been an exponential rise in the And I think the last two years have been difficult. But does seed and pre -seed even make sense as an asset class? And why are you, you know, so bullish or not?

[SPEAKER_01]
I mean, if you ask the companies that in our portfolio that are now, you know, much later stage,

[None]
they'll say

[SPEAKER_01]
that, you know, whether it was me or it was, you know, some other pre -seed or angel back them when no one else would.

[None]
So,

[SPEAKER_01]
yes, there's a whole cohort of founders that are second time founders and they can command capital from lots of people. But I'd say our sweet spot first time founders who have, you know, big visions that maybe most people don't kind of get. They need the support early on. to be able to be kind of the first believer, not just writing the check, but kind of moving them into a community that can support them is, you know, incredibly necessary and rewarding. So there's very few startups, I think, that can just bootstrap and then go to a series A. Potentially, there is that cohort in places like San Francisco. But I'd say for the vast majority of startups, the capital, the community, the content, it's all kind of that early support that founders need.

[SPEAKER_00]
Interesting. And, you know, in my operating experience, I worked with a founder who was a Thiel fellow and another one was a Forbes 30 under 30. When you're looking for a first time founder, are you looking for somebody who is very experienced or are you looking for somebody who is young and scrappy and would want to learn more into that market?

[SPEAKER_01]
I wish I had the perfect archetype to talk about. Then my job would be a lot easier. I of and, you know, the whole industry would be, I think, transformed. The truth is we have everything in our portfolio. We have second time founders, first time founders. We have founders that have worked in the industry for 15 years. We have founders that are, I mean, we have a company called Pair Eyewear. I think we met these founders. were still in university. So we backed them while they were still students. So we have everything in between and we actually haven't seen a lot of patterns. I think the things that we're looking for are founders who have a secret about a world that maybe doesn't exist today. And so you can get that from life experiences. You can get that from work experiences. You can get that from, you know, maybe your imagination. But, you know, those are the types of companies and founder personas that we're looking for. So, yeah, you can solve problems today that are, you know, obvious, right? And those companies get backed and those are good businesses. But I think as venture capitalists, for the most part, we're kind of looking for those crazy outliers that see something that we don't see. And they're able to, through kind of first principles and, you know, some type of analytic framework, explain why the world is getting there. And why they're the right ones to pursue this opportunity. And so those are the real interesting archetypes. And unfortunately, no rhyme or reason who they are. Experienced, old, young. We've seen it all and we've backed it all. We have about 300 companies in our portfolio. So we try to do a lot of kind of looking at looking back and trying to see themes and trends. And on that particular one, we don't see a huge theme.

[SPEAKER_00]
Hmm. And what are your thoughts on follow on investments? Do you think it makes sense to keep an allocation for following investments?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, it's interesting. I think my my thought on this has changed a little bit. So in kind of 2020 through 2022, we made the decision to do follow ons to take all of our pro rata and do SPVs or offer that to RLPs in different formats. And mostly that was because the pre -seed rounds were almost like skipping a stage. So if we would invest in a company, you know, at the pre -seed and say it was a six million valuation, the next round we would see wouldn't be 12. It wouldn't even be 18. It would go to like 25. So we'd say to ourselves like, okay, we write small collaborative checks. If we write another small check, you know, at a 25 million post money valuation, the ownership is so small that we're actually better off of taking another bet in a different company using that cash for a new bet. In the last, you know, two years, 18 months, I'd say the market has shifted a little bit. And so now we see companies kind of raising pre -seeds maybe at that same level, but, you know, their next round, call it a, you know, a seed might be at a 12 post or a 15 post or a 16 post. And at that point, it actually can make sense to double down, you know, depending on your fund model. So it's something that we think through quite a bit. We, I would say, discuss strongly in our partnership of whether we want to do follow -ons, but a lot of it just comes down to kind of the math and whether the valuations make sense. So I'm a little bit mixed on it. For all the funds that we've done, we've only done one check.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_01]
this will be our third fund that we go out and raise in 2025. And we've been a one check only. But it is something that we discuss quite heavily now that the market has shifted.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And, you know, as of recording, we just had Donald Trump come in. TikTok was banned, but now it looks like, you know, it's going to come on. So I don't know what more surprises are going to be there, but I'm hoping the liquidity is going to improve and we'll have a lot more M &As and IPOs coming up. But when it comes to exit strategies and liquidity events, when do you get to decide when to sell your position in a fund?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, it's a great question. I also think there's like a little bit of a misperception that like 2024 and 2023 were like terrible years for M &A. Actually, 2024 was one of the best years for M &A in the last decade. So there was a lot of M &A. It's just that I think the big shiny deals that got blocked by the regulators kind of took the forefront and everyone said, oh, my goodness, like what are exit strategies? If our IPO market is shut and our M &A market is kind of hampered by regulation. The truth is there were a lot of exits that happened.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_01]
in 2024, we returned more capital than we ever have in seven years of running the fund. So there are off ramps. And I think that, you know, you bring up a good point, which is like, when do you sell your shares? And, you know, that's a very personal decision based

[None]
on the fund

[SPEAKER_01]
and the fund model. So

[None]
if

[SPEAKER_01]
you're running a billion dollar fund, right, if you're Andreessen Horowitz, you don't have a ton of off ramps because you have a huge amount of, you know, cash that you need to pay back to your LPs. So for you to get a decent multiple, you need to, you know, cling on to your winners till the till the very end, which would be, you know, an M &A transaction or an IPO. When you're a small fund, when you're a $25 million fund, you actually have a lot more off ramps at later stage, at the later stage. And so we've been able to do some really nice secondaries and return money to our LPs, which makes everyone happy. And it obviously puts more money in the system so that they can reinvest. So it's not a statement on whether we love these companies or, you know, our feeling. It's really just a business model that works for us, which is being able to provide liquidity to our LPs along the way, as opposed to waiting the 10 to 12 years for this kind of monumental exit. And so it's I take it back to like a real personal personal approach for us. It works to be able to do secondaries along the way.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And especially when it comes to pre -send and see startups, know, I worked in startups with not being able to hit the product market fit. But how do you truly analyze product market fit? And what advice will you give to founders, especially with with AI coming in and new tools like Cursor and Lovable? You know, it's easy to make products. But how do you truly analyze the product market fit in the market?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, we're investing pre -product market fit. So we don't spend a ton of time on that. But let's just say if it's a follow on investment or

[None]
something of that

[SPEAKER_01]
that nature. You know, I've been a multi time founder and I think, you know, it's it is kind of what you say. It's it's you know when you see it, right? Because there's just so much incredible appetite for for your product that you can't, you know, barely keep up with with demand. So when you start getting the pull of inbound opportunities, I think you start approaching the product market fit, right? So all your friends and family have brought the product already. Now you're like, you know, super believers have bought the product already. Those those two rings are probably not product market fit, you know, but when you start instead of pushing the boulder uphill, you kind of get to that peak where people are finding out about you organically, there's inbound, then you start to kind of approach something really interesting. And I think the the challenge is that there can be missed signals along the way, right? You can catch a trend, for instance, right? And so, you know, maybe a year ago with some of the the generative AI, it seemed like some of these companies had product market fit because people were rushing to the product. You didn't even have to promote it.

[None]
But as you say,

[SPEAKER_01]
there's some false starts because you have things around moats and defensibility and stickiness for some of these products. So I think it's it's really challenging for founders right now. And the real piece of advice I would give is raise enough money that you can get through these, you know, these highs and these lows, and you can really build a sustainable business and control the levers in your business by not overspending. So that means maybe you grow, you know, less quickly, but you really understand the fundamentals in your business and what kind of keeps keeps things chugging along. So, you know, now we're saying to founders, please raise enough for at least 24 months of runway, because there's going to be a lot of kind of learnings, pivots and fastballs that come along the way that we can't even anticipate today. So make sure that you have the runway to get you through.

[SPEAKER_00]

[SPEAKER_01]
Oh, my gosh, I spend a lot of time helping founders fundraise. So as the first check in, you know, I feel like my job is to get them, you know, through that seed round. And I think many founders think that, you know, if they have a product and things start or, you know, are starting to work, that that's enough to fundraise. And I think it takes out the whole kind of human element of what it means to create a an impactful story. Right. And to have a narrative that stands out. So one of the things that I help a lot of our founders with is, you know, they've kind of raised raised their round and they're going out for PR. Right. And so they they think that the the PR pitch is about their fundraise. And what I have to tell them is like no one cares about their fundraise. They care about, you know, something that is contemporary that it's happening in this moment of time and how their product kind of interacts with that. So you mentioned a good one, you know, the tick tock ban and what that will mean, you know, for companies going forward. So if you're going to go out for, you know, PR or even a raise capital, like take that narrative and position your company around kind of what generally is happening today and where you think things are going. So I think the thing that founders miss is that they're very much in their heads about them, their product and maybe their customers. And when you fundraise or do PR or, you know, anything around your company, you need to, like, take a take a zoom out and say, like, why does anyone care? What are people talking about more generally and how do I fit into that? So that's something that we help founders with their their narrative quite a bit.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And, you know, somebody who's raised pre -seed and they're looking to raise their seed round. What is the best way to put their VCs to work so that, you they can get to the next round?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So, you know, getting organized is half the battle.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_01]
I think that's something else that founders underestimate is just how much time it takes to prep

[None]
to run

[SPEAKER_01]
a very meticulous fundraise. So there's two ways to fundraise. There's an opportunistic way, which is, you know, associates from funds start pinging you. And, you know, you're talking to a few people here and there and you start kind of, you know, getting your materials together and you get kind of pulled into a fundraise by someone else. The other way to fundraise is to be very thoughtful and planful that you want to fundraise and figure out how much you want to raise, what your timeline is, who are your kind of ideal investors and really spend, like, a couple of months doing the research on who these people are. Do they write checks in your space? Who's the right person at that firm? What's their thesis? And really kind of be honest with yourself, you know, about who are the best folks for you. Build that list. Be meticulous about keeping it updated. And, you know, to your question, putting your VCs to work. Then get everyone on your cap table, not, you know, not just your VCs, but, you know, your angels, your friends and family to help make those introductions. And so you can run a real meticulous process or you can be dragged into a fundraise that, you know, maybe you want, maybe you don't want, but you just have a lot less control. And I think as founders, we need to kind of take back the control of the fundraise, control, you know, the narrative, the story, the documents and, you know, create the kind of buzz around your fundraising.

[SPEAKER_00]
And should founders always be raising or do you think, you know, three to six months is enough time for them to, you know, get to the next round?

[None]
I

[SPEAKER_01]
mean, I think it's helpful to devote 5 % of your time to maintaining relationships in general. And I say that across fundraising. I say that across PR. say that across, you know, customers like, you know, just spending a little bit of your time cultivating your network makes a lot of sense so that you have a lot of kind of warm entrees into these different areas. So I say always be fundraising a little bit. There's some founders, I think they take it to the extreme, right, where they're, you know, they just closed around and they're spending half their time meeting with new funders and that's like all they're talking about. And, you know, I think your job as a founder to build a business and to, you know, create a product that everyone wants. And if you do that, the money will come. I do think on a practical level, it is helpful to have a good network and connections. And so especially if you don't live in New York or the Bay Area, maintaining that connectivity. So, you know, if you live in a smaller tech ecosystem and you happen to go out to the Bay Area to meet a customer. Yes. Take two or three meetings with investors that might be right for your next round. Don't tell them you're fundraising. Don't use a deck. Just go have a coffee. Right. [SPEAKER_00]

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So as mentioned, we, you know, we've kind of pioneered this thing called community based venture capital. And

[None]
so all

[SPEAKER_01]
our deal flow comes from those 500 founders and operators who are our eyes and ears on the ground. They help us source diligence and ultimately support our large portfolio. in the resilient economy. So what is the underlying software, technology, infrastructure, the kind of scaffolding around the software that helps those verticals be resilient going forward? [SPEAKER_00]

So actually, it's 12 chapters, 12 countries, 12 inspirational founders, and my journeys in those locations. So I have a whole chapter on India.

[None]
I

[SPEAKER_01]
have an amazing founding team from Trachin that I interview. And when you hear these stories of how the founders met, of how they decided to do this crazy thing, you know, building a startup, and the conviction that they actually needed to leave their jobs and to do something, you know, totally different, it's very inspiring to me. And so the book is really about celebrating these founder heroes that are far from the glow of Silicon Valley, but they've built these really impactful companies. So it's a narrative nonfiction. I think you'll enjoy it. It takes a trip around the world and really explores startup ecosystems in many locations.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. Yeah, absolutely. I'm really looking forward to reading the book. And Jenny, you've been very active in the New York ecosystem, but what are some of the unique challenges and opportunities that you've observed outside of Silicon Valley? [SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, well, New York was not a great ecosystem when I started my company. So what's been fun about it is to be part of the creation or the evolution of New York. So when I started in 2008, like there was no WeWork, there was no resources for founders, there was really no venture capital. And we saw that all kind of come together. There were venture capitalists and they were all in Mayfair. And all of a sudden we saw, you know, this whole new area and ecosystem develop. And so to be a small part of all of these has been really awesome. And now, you know, we want to see every location become, you know, the next Silicon Valley. And I think with, you know, more dispersion of founders, more wealth being distributed, more platforms like, you know, like this one we're using, Riverside or Slack or, you know, whatever it is, I don't think that you need to be in one location. In fact, people really never know where I am. It's always a big joke whenever I get on a call. People are like, where are you, Jenny? So I could be building the New York ecosystem, but I could be in Australia and you wouldn't even know. And I

[None]
think that's what's

[SPEAKER_01]
magical about right now is the, you know, the digital world and the physical world are really merging in an amazing way. So it's been awesome to be part of the New York ecosystem, tech ecosystem develop. I'm a professor at two universities, Cornell and Columbia, and I just love being able to inspire the next generation of students to go out there and build. And, you know, I'd love to see, you know, more people around the world kind of stitching those things together. Right. So it's academia, it's startups, it's corporates. There's just a lot of players. And I think you need to kind of bear hug them all to really build a really unique startup ecosystem.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. And, you know, you've been in the ecosystem for such a long time and I've seen, you know, new syndicates come up, crowdfunding models. But what are your thoughts on the future of pre -seated investing, especially with AI coming in 2022? How do you see, you know, it evolve in the next coming years?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, I think as investors, we all have access to like much better tools that frees up our time to do things that we want to do. Right. So if we don't have to spend endless amounts of time researching and deal memos and synthesizing information, we can just use Granola to record and, you know, all these great tools, honestly, that frees up my time to do what I love, which is spending time with founders. So I think the way it's going to impact us at, you know, the first level is going to be, it's going to make us much more efficient. And again, as I mentioned at the beginning, running a fund is, there's a lot of infrastructure you need to maintain. So if we can do that more effectively and efficiently, I think that's going to be, you know, great for our time and really for our ability to reach more founders. You know, the second order is a little more interesting. It's like, well, will you actually need VCs? In the same way that I think that conversation is happening, like, well, will you actually need lawyers and will you actually need any service providers? I don't really have the answer except to say that I'm open to the possibility that it all changes, whereas I feel like the lawyers are not open to that. When you tell, when I tell my lawyer friends that the whole empire that they've built may come crumbling down, they look at me like I'm crazy and they don't want to talk to me. Whereas, like, I feel more open to that as a possibility for venture capital, like, maybe I won't have a job in five years. And you know what, like, that's fine. I'll keep on building and going where the interesting opportunities are. So, you know, I think in the short term, not a ton is going to change except hopefully for the better that we have more time

[None]
freed up for

[SPEAKER_01]
founders. In the long term, will there be kind of a marketplace using AI agents that doesn't really require me to be there, that efficient capital can be, you know, connected to great founders? Like, I'm open to that.

[None]
Hmm.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. Interesting. And, you know, I quickly want to do the top three. What's your favorite business book?

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, this is kind of interesting. I just reread The Innovators by Walter Isaacson, and it's an old book, but it gave me a lot of inspiration for the future. So I sometimes think, like, going back and revisiting older books is pretty great.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. put that in the show notes. And, you know, if you could go back in time when you started Everywhere Ventures, what is the one thing you would have focused on or done differently?

[SPEAKER_01]
Oh, my gosh, that's a good question. I think we expanded pretty quickly. And with that, we covered a lot of ground. And so we probably should have been a little bit more planful about where we wanted to go and why. And I think, you know, like many founders, you just, you feel product market fill. You feel the pull of different geographies. And all of a sudden, like, we wanted to be there. So maybe a little bit more planning on how we rolled out Everywhere Ventures everywhere.

[SPEAKER_00]
And

[None]
what's

[SPEAKER_00]
your favorite online tool, for example, Gmail, Slack, Zoom, Chargipity?

[SPEAKER_01]
We run our whole community on Slack.

[None]
So we

[SPEAKER_01]
have a thousand founders. We've exchanged more than one million Slack messages since we started it. And zero cat memes. It's all founder resources. So there's a lot of fancy tools out there. But that one is really critical for us.

[SPEAKER_00]
Got it. We'll put that in the show notes. And Jenny, what's the best way people can reach out to you and know more about your book?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, so you can connect with me on LinkedIn. And Venture Everywhere is out soon. So check it out on Amazon. And that's it. Follow me on Twitter.

[SPEAKER_00]
Awesome. We'll put down the show notes. Jenny, thank you so much for taking the time speaking to us. I really enjoyed my conversation with you.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thank you, Rohit. This was great.

My name is Ron Gonan, and I'm a MBA grad from Columbia Business School, and I also teach a course on social entrepreneurship here in the spring. So we have a large panel, so I'm going to go ahead and start down that way in terms of just introductions and a brief bio.

[SPEAKER_02]
Hello, everyone. My name is Ximena Mendarez. I was most recently the chief product officer at OkCupid, leading many different teams. We IPO'd last year. Before that, I worked at Meetup, Zynga, Facebook, and Eventbrite. And before that, I've worked in Europe for many years, grew up in Mexico.

Hey, my name is Jimmy Chen. I'm the founder and CEO of Propel. We aim to make the food stamp program more user -friendly through software. I was previously a product manager at Facebook, and before that a product manager at LinkedIn.

[SPEAKER_07]
I'm Chris Davis. I'm the CFO of Managed by Q. Our mission is to make the world work better. How that manifests itself right now is we provide services to small and medium -sized businesses. Hi, I'm Jenny Fielding. I'm managing director at Techstars. We're a venture capital fund, and we're on our third fund. We also run accelerator programs, 24 of them globally. And you probably know Startup Weekend. We acquired that last year, and so now we're running Startup Weekend in, I believe, countries worldwide. But I look at two verticals. I invest in Internet of Things and FinTech, and I've invested in about 100 companies over my career.

[SPEAKER_00]
I'm Chris Grew. I'm the CEO and founder of American Prison Data Systems. We are a New York City -based tech startup. We are also a public benefits corporation. Our mission is to provide tools to the folks who run America's very large, very expensive, and arguably dysfunctional correctional systems with tools that help them improve safety, the efficacy of their spend, and most importantly, that work towards delivering better outcomes for incarcerated people. Prior to this, I've been an entrepreneur of one kind or another in the U.S. K -12 educational publishing space, where I have started businesses and worked as an entrepreneur in residence at some large American publishing companies, including Scholastic, the Princeton Review, a handful of others, and I'm also proud to say I'm a Columbia alum.

[SPEAKER_06]
Thank you, everybody, for joining the panel. Jimmy, I'd like to start with you. You've had the experience of working at two of the largest tech companies in terms of just serviceability and access to the larger public in terms of your experience at LinkedIn and Facebook. Talk a little bit about your experience at both of those companies and their focus on being expansive, as well as what were some of the limitations that you saw or maybe some areas where they didn't recognize there was opportunity or focus, and then maybe transition that into some of the lessons you've learned there that you want to take into your current early -stage startup.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yeah, so prior to starting this company, I led kind of the traditional Silicon Valley career. I studied computer science at Stanford. I went to work at these kind of different tech companies in Silicon Valley, and these are amazing companies full of really smart people doing kind of really big things, but by and large, the role of the 10,000th employee at Facebook is to increase the number of minutes that someone spends clicking on pictures of cats. That's right. I think that one of the challenges with Silicon Valley as it exists today is that by and large, you've got a lot of companies that are focused on solving the problems that the founders of tech startups have, and so there are tons and tons of companies out there focused on ways to order lunch or ways to clean your room or ways to play games, and there aren't a lot of companies out there that solve kind of the social problems that we see throughout America. And so that's how we started Propel in 2014 in Brooklyn to bring some of the top -tier software development practices of Silicon Valley to an industry and to a set of users that traditionally don't have very good software, and for us, that's people on food stamps.

[SPEAKER_06]
Great. you.
