How many products or services have you seen out there where you kind of step back and say, wow, these guys are really solving a problem for a group that no one's really paid attention to, and there could be a great opportunity here?

[SPEAKER_03]
Yeah, so what's interesting about Techstars, because we see so many startups, so we work on, you know, for our accelerators around applications, right? And so if you look at my last program, Internet of Things, we had over a thousand applications, and so that really affords us an opportunity to kind of front -run trends that you're seeing more generally, right? Because we can look at the data, you know, in aggregate and say, wow, these are new areas that are popping up. And so those are kind of like micro -trends, and it's really fun for us to kind of get ahead of that. But I think to your point, you know, we are looking for entrepreneurs that are solving real problems, and I would say, you know, the majority of our applications are nice to have, not must have. And so, you know, we spend a lot of time with the entrepreneurs making sure that, you know, not only is there product market fit, but there's founder market fit, and it kind of aligns with our core beliefs at Techstars.

[SPEAKER_06]
Okay. This is going to come up in a follow -up question for two of the entrepreneurs on the panel here in a second. But my sense is that because the investment community is sometimes so focused on what's hot today, as an entrepreneur, if you're actually really solving a problem for somebody, there's a pain point, but it's not the hot thing today, what recommendation would you provide in terms of how they communicate that to a potential investor VC to help them see the light?

[SPEAKER_03]
Yeah. I mean, I think an accelerator is a great way to go because we're not really looking for those hot trends. We're looking for entrepreneurs. So we always say, you know, we invest in these six things in this order, team, team, team, product, you know, market, and, you know, a few other things. So, you know, we're really looking for awesome teams of entrepreneurs, and I think that that affords the opportunity to, you know, differentiate yourself with something that's ahead of the curve. And so we've taken, you know, an active role. I'd say three years ago we started investing in, like, frontier tech. So we have a large portfolio of AR and VR and robotics and some of these things that, you know, now have become very popular. So I think, you know, if you go with early -stage investors like us, we're really willing to look beyond the traditional.

[None]
Great. Thank you.

[SPEAKER_06]
Ximena, OKCupid. It's always great to have somebody from a dating service on a panel. So many

[None]
questions people

[SPEAKER_06]
want me to ask you, right? But my sense is that when you come to a dating site and you're getting it launched, there can be a tendency to gravitate towards what society views as a typical dating profile or the typical type of person who's going to ask somebody out and who wants to be asked out by them. But in fact, especially in the United States and especially in major urban areas, there's a lot of diversity out there in terms of preferences, what people are looking for. And, you when it's online, there's a lot more flexibility and confidence that someone can have. What did you guys do at OKCupid to make sure you didn't gravitate towards, let's just facilitate something for the status quo dating or the stereotype dating? And how do we make this more expansive to get business in from lots of diverse groups and their preferences?

[SPEAKER_02]
So I'm going to start with dating tips because I'm sure you're going to find them interesting. In terms of we actually found on OKCupid that there's, of course, a lot of people that get a lot of likes. That's the people that, on average, everyone thinks that they're good looking. Those people will get X number of messages. But what is really interesting is the people that are found to be polarizing. So either a big set of people will think they're really bad looking and other people will think that they're really good looking. The reason is that the people that find them really good looking will find them so compelling. It's almost like they find that special match that no one else could see that they had all this potential. So when we talk about what are recommendations for our profiles is that it should not be the thing that you think everyone will like. You need to write about the things that make you different. Like from all the quirks of, like myself, I like to do hand crafting for jewelry or things that are just a bit odd. And then there might be someone that really, that resonates with them. So that's the part about if a profile is detailed, it has more chances of getting that special someone that just is intrigued by the thing that you're writing, even if it's a little bit weird. The second part is about not just going by the masses. So at OKCupid, I'll talk about it a little bit later, we took the stance to also launch 22 genders and 13 orientations. And that was a big decision from the business side because we knew that it was not going to be used by a lot of people and most of the dating is just going to be men, women, and then gay, straight, and bisexual. But then we decided that if it's something so important to people, like who's going to be the person that you might marry, you need to use the words that feel appropriate. So when someone in Kansas, a boy that is 18 years old, can write questioning sexuality, all of a sudden it has the people when they see it, it's something that it's OK. And then you can say, well, there's so many things about my sexuality that I'm still figuring out. Or in terms of genders, these are all the different genders I align with. So that was more from when you're thinking of a business, it's not for everyone, but it's also about the social responsibility that you have towards the people so that you're advancing towards where society is going and that sometimes it's not just about the bottom line or revenue, but what should be good.

[SPEAKER_06]
Great. Thank you. Next two questions are related to Chris and Christopher, and I'll ask Christopher to answer this first and then Christopher to follow up. One of the challenges I can imagine about both of your businesses is you're dealing with a labor force that the perception is can be a little bit challenging in terms of showing up on time, delivering service in terms of your space. Is that a perception that you struggle with or not? And talk a little bit about just dealing with the labor force that you deal with, how you convince your customer that, hey, we're going to provide great service, we're always going to be on time, so on and so forth.

[SPEAKER_07]
Well, I think it really starts from the heart of Q. I mean, when Q was being developed, we looked at a slate of services and a client of small to medium -sized businesses, and we said, okay, how can we solve a problem for this potential client? And then in looking at that client over a bunch of services, cleaning, for example, we realized that in the cleaning industry, there's a huge client churn. They churn their cleaning operators a lot every year, but then there's also huge operator churn. We call everyone operators at Q. Huge operator churn every year, and we realized that those two things were connected. So you couldn't solve one problem without also trying to solve the other problem. So at Q, we decided to take on trying to create a better work experience for the operator, and that would actually create a better client experience, and the two are linked. So it's not that we go out to the clients and say, hey, our operators are not going to do X. What we've done is we invested in a, you know, it's called a good job strategy. We invested in a program where we invested in sort of recruiting, training, and then developing our operators within their various service lines, and then we looked at technology to help them do their jobs better and also how to communicate back and forth with, you know, oh, I'm going to be late because the subway's down. It's not that you're late. It's that you can communicate to the client that you're going to be late or you are unable to perform a task, so it's not like you're leaving the office space with a task unperformed. The client then knows through technology that, oh, this task was performed because the dishwasher was broken. So it's combining technology not only for the service of the client but also for the service of the operator to make the whole thing work better.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_06]
it sounds like you've taken, you've used technology and taken what most people viewed as a cost and an obstacle, and you've taken technology and turned that perceived cost and perceived obstacle into a major financial opportunity for your company and everyone involved.

[SPEAKER_07]
I mean, we think so because in certain industries, the business in this industry spent a lot of money on replacing revenue for lost clients and spending money on hiring new people for lost operators. And what we looked at is, hey, by investing more money up front to create a better product and a better experience for our employees, we're actually then able to spend that money on growing the business, not replacing the business lost.

[None]
Great. Related

[SPEAKER_06]
to that, Christopher, just so everyone's clearly aware, your core market are hardcore prisoners, right? People have been put away because of something bad that they did in society. And you've decided to design a product and service that is going to help them rehabilitate themselves and be more productive citizens in society. Sounds like a big waste of time. These guys completely screwed up. They're sitting in prison. What do you think in trying to give them a tablet and technology to do something with?

[SPEAKER_00]
Oh, there's a lot there. The first thing is, you know, America incarcerates more people than any civilization has in its history, more than the gulag state. And it's a mixed bag of who ends up incarcerated. There are 2.2 million people behind bars today, another 5.5 million on parole or probation, which means 1 out of every 31 adults in the United States is behind bars. And for every Charles Manson that we lock up and never want to see again and I've sort of given up on, there are lots and lots and lots of folks who've just made bad decisions, ended up in bad circumstances, and hopefully have a bright future ahead of them. And the mission of our business is to, to the maximum extent possible, give people a second chance. The vast majority of people who are incarcerated in the United States will be released and they will be back living with us and we'll see them on the subway. And it's in everyone's best interest that they have the tools that they need to succeed. And so what we're trying to do is use technology to deliver individualized education, rehabilitation, job training, and re -entry skills so that folks who have made bad decisions and maybe have been left behind by the school system or other parts of society have an opportunity to start their lives again. And I'm struck by some of the congruences and possible opportunities to work together with Jimmy's business and with Chris's. So, one, we shouldn't give up on these folks. Two, they're extremely, it's an extremely diverse set. And what we need to do as a mission of our business is, paradoxically, we have taken a large bunch of people who have a very diverse set of education, rehabilitation, job training, and re -entry needs, and we've isolated them in the last part of American society where technology cannot reach them. And we've sort of unintentionally put a digital mode around them, which is separating them from the kinds of programs that could really make a difference in their lives. So the mission of our business has been to build a bridge across that mode to allow all of the wonderful things that technology can do, all of those educational programs, to drive across that bridge, but also at the same time safeguard public safety by making sure that, you we don't have inmates on Twitter or on Facebook or even OKCupid, I'm sorry to say, until they're out and released and then that might be a good thing for them to be doing with their time.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_06]
let's talk dollars and cents, right, because you're a for -profit venture. How much does it cost to incarcerate somebody in the United States?

[SPEAKER_00]
Let's start top down. The direct cost of incarceration in the United States are at least $85 billion annually. We've already talked about the numbers of people we incarcerate. So locking up that many people and spending $85 billion a year averages $30,000, $35,000 a year to incarcerate someone, depending on where you are. Here in New York City, it's at least $110,000 a year. In

[None]
Mississippi, it's a little expensive than going

[SPEAKER_06]
to Columbia.

[None]
It's much more expensive than going

[SPEAKER_00]
to Columbia. And all of that might be OK if the system, quote -unquote, worked. And what do we mean by working in corrections? Making the public safer and hopefully changing lives where that's possible. We have a 43 % recidivism rate in this country, which means of the 800,000 people who will be released from prison in the United States, 43 % of them will be back in prison within three years. So it's not working. And though we have dramatically increased the number of people that we've incarcerated, we have not seen concomitant improvements in public safety or decreases in violence. So what we're doing isn't working, and it's expensive. And so our goal is to be disruptive and to create new tools. The folks who run our correctional institutions are, in general, very well motivated to give the public what they want. They just haven't had the tools to do that. And that's where I see a for -profit, for -purpose business sort of getting in.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_06]
it costs $100,000 in New York City to keep somebody in prison. What are you charging the system to provide education and professional training services to this person so that when they get out of prison, they're not returning because you've given them the skills?

[SPEAKER_00]
We're in 20 locations across the country. I'm very proud to say that one of those locations is Rikers Island. I'll get very specific about that. We work with all of the juveniles who are in something called East River Academy, which is a high school that's run on Rikers Island. And we work with a good portion of the young adults and some of the highest risk offenders. The average cost is about $1,200 a license seat. And though the most concrete version of our business is people say, oh, you sell tablets. Well, we are, in fact, we are a software -as -a -service business. And what matters is not the device itself, but the content that's delivered. And it's very important because this is sort of brass tack stuff. We have to sit down on day one and say, if you invest $1,000 in a software -as -a -service license seat for this inmate, let me show you how that will save you, Mr. Warden, $3,000 in the first year. And that's enough to get over the first threshold. Over time, we hope to have the longitudinal data that suggests that we get at the real cost center and the real benefit, that is we're reducing recidivism. And a 5%, 10 % decrease in recidivism in this country would save state and local and federal institutions and taxpayers billions of dollars. Okay, great. Thank you.

[SPEAKER_06]
Jimmy, I'd like to

[None]
bring

[SPEAKER_06]
that. Okay.

[None]
I

[SPEAKER_02]
actually had a point exactly around that. That was, I've lately been seeing a lot of trends on companies that could do things more efficiently. So, for instance, for the government of New York City to transport people that are handicapped, it's really expensive because they need to have the schedule, they need to go pick them up, and it's just, it's something that is really inefficient. So, for instance, right now they're collaborating or starting a program with Uber where they can say, we can actually do the transportation more efficiently because we don't need to hire, buy the trucks and hire the drivers and do all the infrastructure around it.

[None]
But I think I'm

[SPEAKER_02]
even more interested in, I've been talking, I talked last week with the CEO of a company called Joyable, and they do mental health programs. And I was really excited because they're basically using technology for something that has so much stigma. Like, people actually don't like to talk about depression or other mental issues that they have. And if you think about Duolingo, that's a personalized tool that allows you to learn something. Well, in the same way, they can do programs now that allow you to talk about the problems that you could have and over time accomplish a lot of the, it's almost like going to therapy without actually having to even go outside of your door and they're trying to reach people that don't even want to talk about the problems that they have. So, talking because it's a tech panel, I think that what it's exciting is that you have people like Jimmy building companies that are helping people, but also that technology is not only now as it was before social media, and then it went to fintech or health tech, but it's also addressing issues that the society has. So, over time, tech will just be a means towards helping people in more efficient ways.

[None]
Sure.

[SPEAKER_06]
And Jimmy, you have a similar business model where today there's a major societal cost around food stamps, and you've recognized that pain point. Talk a little bit about just the pure economics of your business because today the industry and the base that you're focusing on, think a lot of Americans would just view it as, it's a cost, it's inefficient. Talk about the economics of how you're able to create a for -profit business and a social good.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yeah, so let me start with the size of the program. There are 45 million Americans on food stamps today, so every table in this room has about seven chairs. That's about one chair at every table is somebody who's on food stamps. Combined, the food stamp program is about $70 billion each year. This is money that ends up being spent at grocery stores. about 12 % of the American retail grocery industry is actually food stamps. It's a huge industry because there are a ton of people who kind of experience it, and their day -to -day experience with the program turns out is not very good. Now, I think if you've gone to the DMV or applied for a visa, you probably have a sense that, you know, interacting with a government website or filling out a paper form can be really frustrating. I can tell you the same is true for a single mother who's trying to apply for food stamps or somebody who has benefits and is trying to understand how to best use their food stamps. So our core product is actually just a smartphone app. It's an app called Fresh EBT that works a little bit like mint.com for people on food stamps. So it helps people understand their current balance to see their transaction histories and to create these budgets that help them stretch their benefits to where they want to be. Our business comes from helping our users to discover other products and services that make them more physically and financially healthy. And so there's kind of two categories of that. The first one are kind of grocery stores. So last month, our users spent about $40 million combined in food stamps at grocery stores. How do we use that combined purchasing power to get them savings on the food that they're already going to purchase? Our second business model is financial service referrals. So we have a population that's traditionally preyed on pretty significantly by the financial services industry. But we think there's a large and growing segment of companies out there building pro -social financial services that can replace some of these old, stodgy financial services that would just aim to rip people off. So these are things like online replacements for payday loans or for check cashing or for title loans. How do we introduce our users to those things in a way that makes them more financially healthy?

[SPEAKER_06]
So I see an interesting thread taking place here. think oftentimes when you go to a lot of panel discussions about entrepreneurship to the earlier point about most people are trying to solve problems that are issues for themselves or their friends. And they may be masked in, like, I'm changing the world. In fact, they're just trying to make their life a little bit better. Prior to launching her own fund, Jenny spent seven and a half years as the managing director of Techstars, where she invested in a portfolio of companies with a current market cap of over 10 billion. Jenny is a two times founder, a lawyer by training and an adjunct professor at Columbia University and Cornell Tech and author, which I'd love to for you to tell us more about. [None]
interesting journeys,

[SPEAKER_01]
which I'll talk about later in the book. But I started much more, let's call it traditional for someone who grows up in New York. I went to law school, I worked in finance, and I was kind of on on a track. And then in 2007, so about 15 years ago, I had a problem, like a personal thing that I wanted to solve in the world. third startup,

[SPEAKER_00]
I never think I can do anything by myself. I always rely on individuals who have skill set that's different to me and I've always surrounded myself with good talent. You go through your business career and you know you've got to a certain level and are making influence change that gives you a different opportunity lens. For me the exposure that I received during my Eisenhower Fellowship were really looking at how do you ensure that there are the new leaders coming into the world? How do you ensure that there are new businesses that come into the world? And I saw there is an opportunity for venture capital, there is an opportunity for an accelerator incubator and along with Jeevan we sort of thought of this for three years before it came alive. What we do here is we encourage people to learn from each other. As a startup you're always looking at the rupees and cents but you sometimes can't afford to recruit the best people in each area. When you're a startup with two or three people and you have this community suddenly you're not not alone. I've seen people just have grab a coffee, I've seen people playing FIFA football and talking about their business at the same time. So that's what we do here we try and connect people. So for us if we can see companies graduate from when they're three people to twenty people to fifty people to a hundred people that's what really ticks the box and says okay we've helped these people. Anytime you leave a corporate job that you're very well looked after, you like the company, you like the individuals you work with, it's a massive risk because you're leaving a comfort factor. Most people at my age would prefer to just hang tight for another ten years and take retirement on their stride. So I think you know the way I see it if I don't do this now at 44 I will not be able to do this at 55. If you're ever comfortable in changing jobs or even changing houses or changing countries you have to feel a little risky and you have to feel uncomfortable otherwise it's not really changed.

[SPEAKER_01]
Jameson Duttweiler Co -Founder and CEO of Phantasmo. We're building an open platform to 3D map every building on earth. So this is the map data that we have today. It's carried us pretty well to this point, but there's a problem. If you're playing Pokemon Go, it doesn't know if it's on the ground, if it's on a table, or if it's a gigantic character in the middle of a baseball field. The issue here is that our devices don't have any concept of the layout of our spaces. We need 3D data, and thankfully, our mobile devices are getting 3D sensors, as well as six -degree of freedom tracking, or SLAM, on them now. This is the first commercially available Google Tango phone, there's quite a few more coming out this summer and this fall, with Apple not too far behind. You're looking at about 20 % market ratio by 2020 for all phones. So, okay. So, who's Phantasmo? First, we're a pretty stacked team with three PhDs with a lot of very relevant publications. We've had two exits under our belts, and we surround ourselves with some great advisors in the location and mapping space. We really have three key things that make up what we do. We have a spatial mapping SDK in cloud, an open spatial map database and API, and a solution for large -scale spatial mapping. So, the first part, let's focus on that. This is Elon on our team in my living room. He's actually got our SDK on the Google Tango phone there. You see that on the left side. He quickly maps out the space. He does this in about three minutes. So, what ends up happening here is you get this not -so -beautiful looking point cloud. Our pipeline cleans this up, then we segment it out, and we're able to identify the floors, the walls. We're able to segment out the furniture. We're moving towards semantic labeling understanding of the space, and then we create even sort of a simplified storage format to access the structure of the data, as well as meshes. One of our customers, Joybird, is using this to help their customers visualize their furniture inside of people's own homes to see if a couch fits and what it looks like. Okay. The second part is an open spatial map database and API. So, not only do have the SDK that people can use at home, we can go into, say, a Starbucks who asks us to come into their uh, reserve store in LA and create a demo for them. This is a map that we created. Uh, took us about, it takes about 15 or 20 minutes. We actually just read this in a store here in New York, and we're showing a demo of this, uh, to them tomorrow. Uh, and what you do is you take that point cloud, you can download it through our API or from our web platform, you can drop it into Unity, and then you can place spatially referenced content inside the space. You can then push that out to a Google Tango -enabled phone and eventually iOS phones, and you can actually, this is a screen recording from the phone, by the way, you can have the spatially anchored content that you can see throughout the space. So, Starbucks is interested. They're looking at how they increase engagement in stores and tell the story of the products that are inside of here. The pipeline to get to this demo is ours. You know, if you had to do this on your own, this would be weeks, if not months. Okay. So, the last part is the large -scale spatial mapping. Obviously, using a phone to walk around and scan a very large space is not going to be efficient. So, we're able to import data from LiDAR -based devices such as this in combination with other data that we collect with these mobile devices. We then create profiles for these online in a GitHub -like fashion. It can be public, can be private. The owner of the data has complete control over how it's used and who has access to it. So, not only can they build first -party applications on this, but if you go back to that example of Pokemon Go, that Niantic, who publishes Pokemon Go, could request access to the space, this space or Starbucks, and they could grant access to them so that they could actually create content that's aware of the environment. So, our mission is to spatially map every building on Earth, democratize mapping buildings of all sizes, and to be the location DNS. And thank you, Evan, for that one.

[None]

[None]
Yeah,

[SPEAKER_01]

And so I think what founders are feeling is that while back in 2020, 2021, you could get to something like a million dollars in ARR and be able to raise a proper Series A from a great Series A fund. There was a lot of variables on that, what area you're building in, your team background, all those things. But let's just call that general. And fast forward to today, where the goalposts have really moved. And so the tweet was really what I'm kind of seeing, which is the million has now gone up to sometimes three million. [SPEAKER_02]

Right.

At Innovations Everywhere, we help corporates understand innovation trends and engage in the startup world in a meaningful way.

[SPEAKER_01]
To better understand how disruption is happening today, we have scanned the top 50 tech accelerators in the world and due diligence to more than 400 startups looking at their business models, technology and the industries they intend to revolutionize. The general conclusions we came across are 65 % of top ranked accelerators were launched in North America, 25 % in Europe and only 5 % in Asia. 80 % of them were launched between 2010 and 2013. Surprisingly, traditional business models like products and services sales stay dominant, despite the digital revolution. IoT, VR, AR, blockchain and machine learning technologies are not used a lot yet by the latest startups. Those conclusions are based on the analysis of two types of accelerators, major generalist accelerators and corporate accelerators. The industries that startups disrupt the most are IT, health tech, fintech, retail and transport. Let's have a closer look at each one of them. IT startups mostly offer business services solutions, communication solutions and individual service solutions. Health tech startups offer personal or medical devices as their main products. FinTech startups mainly disrupt payments, individual and SME financial services. In the retail sector, we found two types of startup solutions, e -commerce platforms and services to merchants. Mobicon is a good example of a retail startup disrupting the industry.

The realities of climate change could be daunting, yet I remain optimistic. What gives me hope is seeing all of the amazingly talented people addressing the challenges facing us. Our accelerator invests in technology entrepreneurs building businesses where the business model and the impact model are intrinsically linked. When the startup scales, so does the impact. Three months ago, we began program in Boulder, Colorado in person. In the last two months, we've been fully virtual. You're about to see an amazing group of founders addressing climate change in ways that are aligned with the Nature Conservancy's shared conservation mission.

[SPEAKER_07]
For the last four years, the Nature Conservancy has partnered with Techstars to demonstrate what happens when the world's best problem -solving entrepreneurs bring technology solutions to create a sustainable world we know is possible.

[SPEAKER_04]

You're stuck, but you're not alone. 65 % of consumers want to make better purchasing decisions, but only 26 % end up doing so because it's inconvenient and they're not sure how. Finch decodes these products' environmental impacts and encourages consumers to make better purchasing decisions. Using thousands of data points and a variety of trusted resources, we've rated over 80 categories and 70,000 products. Here, you download the extension onto Chrome and you see any product score based on what it's made of, how it's used, and how long it lasts. We are the right team to do this. I have been determined to find sustainability solutions in the consumer space for the past 15 years, informed by my experience at Unilever on their supply chain team and on their sustainability team, and at Yale getting my MBA and master in environmental management. Jane comes from Parachute, an extremely successful direct -to -consumer company, where she understood firsthand the challenges with getting user -facing data to inform better business decisions. Mark recently finished his postdoc at Princeton University in climate research and environmental engineering. Remember that academic study I alluded to earlier? Mark probably wrote it, and he agrees it's kind of tough to get through. Finally, John has decades of experience in software development, and he's making sure that we have a technical, robust solution. We generate revenue by providing data to corporations via a license or data integration API. Companies are hoping to better understand the impacts at scale and how consumers are reacting to sustainability marketed products. Between sustainability consulting, product insights, and market research, this is an $11 billion opportunity. Finch has the ability to tap 65 % of the population who are looking for the same solution to sustainability that NerdWall had solved for personal finance. And right now that doesn't exist, and Finch is so excited to take that space. We've built trust with over 2,000 early adopters through organic community building. We're currently in conversations with three Fortune 500 companies. We have the financial support of the co -founder of Honey, a browser extension with over 10 million monthly active users, and have been featured in Apartment Therapy, Katie Couric Media, and Fast Company, to name a few. If every household in the United States replaced their conventional toilet paper with recycled, we would save 423,000 trees today. Think of the possibilities. Head to choosefinch.com and let us do the heavy lifting so that you don't have to.

This is not only a necessity, but also the largest wealth creation opportunity any of us have seen. The climate tech sector will produce a thousand unicorns in the coming decades. Yet, the upsides are mostly limited to a privileged few. My name is Manuela. I'm CEO at Climatescape, the investment platform for the climate generation. We give everyone a chance to own a piece of the world's most promising climate startups. Anyone can download our app, set personal investment and impact goals, receive a notification with opportunities that match them, learn about companies and technologies, see who was participating in the deal, and invest what's right for you. Over time, you build a diverse portfolio of companies that benefit people and planet. Our service is free for investors. We charge a percentage fee of the capital raised and take stakes from companies in our platform. No more investing alone and being overwhelmed by hundreds of ESG funds and crowdfunding websites with questionable impact. With Climatescape, you become part of a community and can easily invest in solutions verified by experts and aligned with your values. We give you ownership of a sustainable future. You can help companies improve their impact, build their brand, hire, attract clients, and become a successful investment for you and the planet. We scout leading climate startups and enable them to raise up to $5 million from their stakeholders and our community, which will grow through high -quality content, referrals, and targeted marketing. We already built a directory with 2,000 climate startups and 300 community users. Next year, launch our investment app, then expand to Europe and enable secondary market transactions, bringing liquidity to our investors. In the future, companies that raise with Climatescape will mature and go public, who will be well -positioned to go beyond private securities and tap into the trillion -dollar retirement market. Me and my co -founder are experts in Climate Tech. I lie at the Climate Tech market intelligence firm, and my book, The Frontiers of Impact Tech, is a landmark publication in this space, based on contributions from 500 leaders from over 30 countries. Brandon spent over 10 years helping startups build world -class software, and he led the world's most comprehensive open directory in Climate Tech. Since 2020, we are in a new era for retail investing, with millions of new users investing for the first time in public companies or digital assets. Now, three out of four millennials want to invest with a positive impact. This year, Climate Tech attracted $32 billion in venture capital, growing five times faster than the rest of the market. In the next 10 years, the world's biggest companies will be climate companies. If you want to invest in a sustainable future and help shape it, join us at Climatescape.

Climatescape time, farmers have had the difficult task of growing enough food to feed a rapidly growing population. It's estimated we'll have another billion people to feed by 2030. As this demand for food continues to grow, our lands are stretched to their limits. Erosion, tillage, and overgrazing degrade the productivity of farms and rangelands. Agriculture expansion threatens native habitats, and climate change increases extreme events that threaten crop yields. It's clear we must find solutions that not only increase food production, but also sustain the health of our communities, our land, and our water. Entire ecosystems are at stake, and one critical solution lies right under our feet. Healthy soil is nutrient -rich, holds more water, and supports crop productivity. It is a natural solution to remove carbon from the atmosphere and store it in the ground. With farming and ranching occurring on roughly 40 % of land around the world, what if our agriculture systems built the health of our soils instead of degrading them? If we focus on improving and revitalizing soil health, we can leverage the natural biodiversity to improve and sustain farmland's vigor and productivity, while maximizing the soil's potential to sequester carbon, and support resilient and profitable growing conditions for farmers. With a change in mindset, there's a global opportunity to support more innovation in soil health. With broad access to better practices and financial incentives, farmers can and will lead the way to a more sustainable future.

This is where Farms2U comes in. We provide farmers with training on what to grow and how, based on data points like where their farm is located or what the soil composition is. Hello, I'm Dr. Carlos Gaitan, CEO of Benchmark Labs, and I'm here to introduce our hyperlocal forecasting technology, a $30 billion opportunity. Weather affects all of us, but can make or break a business in the agricultural sector. Effectively managing pest, frost, heat, labor, and water are dependent on highly accurate weather forecasts. However, the same unreliable approach to weather forecasting has been used for the last 80 years. National weather services divide the globe in big boxes, and everybody inside a box receive exactly the same forecast. This is a non -local approach. But in reality, if you look inside of the boxes, they aggregate a variety of microclimates. For example, here we have two farms in the wine region of Portugal. As you can see, there are changes in elevation, land cover, and water availability, all leading to special microclimates and different farm management practices. Nevertheless, they receive exactly the same forecast for the different microclimates. We are the first and only solution to provide true hyperlocal forecasting. Our technology reduces the forecasting errors from the National Weather Service up to 60%. We do this by integrating third -party hardware and data with our proprietary technology to provide field -specific reports via mobile, web, and our API. Our web and mobile apps show real -time forecasts and information and alerts of all the relevant environmental variables for farm managers. Our significant improvement in forecast accuracy leads to more accurate labor and irrigation management, better pest control, and better frost prevention. We offer a software -as -a -service solution, targeting initially specialty crops and high -value land managers. And our customers and channel partners love us. In this particular case, Benchmark Labs help them reduce applied water by 25 % along with the associated pumping costs. And we enable the creation of new product fosters too. We have farm managers and high -value land managers paying for our solutions. And we just signed a partnership agreement with an insurance marketplace and with hardware manufacturers to supplement our revenue streams. Our technology has also been funded by the National Science Foundation and NASA. We are aware that this opportunity is bigger than specialty crops. When you include energy, insurance, and land management, it is a 30 billion opportunity. We have more than 15 years of experience in environmental forecasting, hardware, analytics, and consulting in both the public and private sectors. And our diverse team is motivated and determined to bring the best service and forecast to the world. Every farm is different. Every field is different. Your farm, your field, your forecast. Benchmark Labs.

You're scared and things happen fast, but you stay focused because the ship can't get back on course until everyone safely lands. You have to rely upon your training, your instruments, and your team to get the job done. Hi, my name is Mike Smith. I lived this experience as an F -18 pilot in the U.S. Navy for 12 years. Though I had a great career, I wanted to do more. I left the Navy to become a carbon market expert and, in the process, developed the largest carbon reforestation project in U.S. history. Now, I'm proud to be leading an incredible team of serial entrepreneurs and technologists at Acclimate, where we steer small businesses through humanity's greatest challenge, climate change. These are turbulent times. Small businesses are being thrust by a rising climate generation to show actions on emissions reductions, but they feel lost without the experience or the guidance they need amidst a sea of carbon accounting tools. At Acclimate, our team of climate navigators provides our customers the direction and the instruments they need to pilot their company to climate neutrality without fumbling in the dark. Our solution begins by conducting customers through a personalized onboarding process before leading them onto the Acclimate platform. Here, they experience powerful integrated carbon accounting and they begin to tangibly understand their footprint. They realize how different we are from other carbon calculators built for deep -pocketed, large corporate sustainability departments. Instead, we provide our small business customers with the expert guidance, affordable accounting, and personal service that they need. We help them to identify where their emissions are coming from and the behaviors causing it. We lead them into emissions reductions. But navigating climate action is more than carbon accounting. And for most of our customers, the next milestone is buying carbon offsets. Our marketplace has an industry -leading selection of offsets from reputable registries with embedded proof of verification from third -party auditors. However, our customers have told us that they need help in making deeper emissions reductions, such as through community solar programs and employee commuting incentives. So our marketplace will expand to include these climate solutions from our growing network of partners. Partners who will create revenue acceleration for Acclimate as our success becomes theirs. This will accelerate our impact, too. We'll help our customers prevent or sequester a half million tons of carbon, which will have secondary effects in water, habitat, and urban and rural development. Our beachhead of impact -focused companies are passionate about what we've created. One of our earliest, Kristen, was able to save the $4,000 she would have spent on a consultant and put it to work in offsetting her company's emissions with us. Her small business gets better data and better marketing, and she looks good to her boss and her coworkers. And Kristen is just one of many who continue to fix their footprint with Acclimate, because they love the product we built on a shoestring better than what our competitors built with millions. The final part of the customer journey is when they can demonstrate action to their employees, their customers, and their communities through marketing and branding. [SPEAKER_00]
All right. Hello, everyone. We are live here on Crowdcast. If you can hear us and see us, go ahead and shout out in the chat. We're super excited to be holding this for the Techstars Network and seeing so many Techstars founders and alumni in the chat. see Italy, London, Buffalo, Pittsburgh. So awesome to have everyone here. And thank you so much for joining us on the short notice. We lost Jenny real quick, but we'll get her back. And for this special edition, AMA on fundraising during a tough market and tough circumstances. So as I tried to find Jenny back online, Eamon, do you want to go ahead and give a little bit of introduction?

[SPEAKER_02]
For sure. Yeah, yeah. How's it going, folks? Good to see. Well, amazing to see so many of you on here. And well, welcome to my kitchen or the adjunct office of Techstars London, as is the case now. It's Jenny back again. So yeah, delighted to see all of you here. Hopefully, I saw some people saying they were 10 days in isolation, some that were seven days. So hopefully, people are doing well, that your families and people around you are healthy as well. We wanted to do this AMA for a couple of reasons, right? Like we get a lot of requests from different people asking for support and help in different ways. And obviously, one of the biggest ones at the moment is exactly what's going on in the kind of investor community. So basically, what we'll do today is, Jenny and I will introduce ourselves. We have got loads of time to answer questions. So kind of somewhere down here, you can stick your questions. The comment section on the right hand side is a little bit more active. So if you put it in the ask a question section, it'll be a little bit easier for us to get through and upload them. But we've got about an hour or so to get through them. And I'm sure if we run over, I'm more than happy to spend a bit more time chatting to people. So to kind of kick things off, the rationale for me sitting here. So my name is Aben. I run the Techstars London program. I've been doing that for the last two and a half years. Previously, we ran our AB InBev program in New York and have been a Techstars mentor since 2013 and an angel investor in over 50 companies now across the US, Europe, Africa and Asia. And founder, so three to two, which were moderate successes and one which was like a massive failure or kind of learning experience, which is the polite way of saying it. The first company I started was back in 2004, back home in Ireland. And we were effectively a company that said yes to other people's requests. So an agency business that built stuff for big corporates. websites, you know, mobile apps when J2ME was still a thing before even iOS and Android existed. And so worked with lots and lots of big corporates and scaled the business out of Ireland into the UK over kind of 2004, 2005 and six, weirdly did some work out in Korea as well. And for those of you who remember the kind of financial crisis started to kick in, certainly the writing started appearing on the wall, the back end of 2007. And then through 2008, it just kept getting worse and and worse and worse and worse. Ireland in particular was hit really badly. The UK hit pretty badly as well. And we went through a situation where effectively over the course of six months, about 80 % of our revenue disappeared. So clients were not renewing contracts. In some cases, people didn't pay their bills. In some cases, some of our clients went bankrupt. So it was a very difficult time. We had to lay people off, we had to, you know, try and be nimble, we had to do as many things as we could ourselves, we have to deal with our own challenges with with banks and, you short term loans that we had and various different things. So an incredibly stressful period. And so I have a lot of empathy with what I'm sure many of you are feeling at the moment. You know, I say it kind of as a joke, but it's also true that I can probably draw you a, you know, inch perfect map of the roof of my bedroom from that I slept in at that stage, because you were just waking up in the middle of night kind of looking at the ceiling going, how are we going to make this work? Are we going to be able to make payroll? Are we going to be able to help people out? So I think two things that kind of lessons learned for for me from from that period were, I think the first one is kind of over, over communicate. And I think that goes kind of across the board. So, you know, certainly from our perspective, we over communicated with staff. So, you know, everyone is feeling uncertain and nervous. And everyone is probably reading Twitter and, you know, getting information from the media that's saying good, bad and indifferent things. And your colleagues are no different. And lots of people will be worrying about their jobs and their futures. And I think the more that you can be transparent and let them know that, you know, there may be cuts and pay cuts and that, you you as a founding team should, you know, ideally be leading from the front in that regard, I think you'll be surprised if you do that and how many people say, yes, I'm willing to take a cut. Yes, I want to stay working with the organization. Yes, I want to stay involved. So I think over communicating with with your team is important. And when it gets to the point, and hopefully it won't for any of you. But if it gets to the point that you have to, you know, lay people off, then I think, use the network that you're part of through Techstars, use the networks that you have around you, you know, one of the things that we try to do is make sure that as many colleagues as possible ended up getting, you know, interviews and opportunities at other places, because obviously, we didn't want people to end up in very bad situations. I think likewise, over communicate with with, you know, anyone who is paying you. So any clients or users or others, you know, we were able to talk to some people who owed us money and get smaller amounts of money from them rather than getting none. We saw some interesting partnership opportunities open up as a result. So over communicating with with clients and customers is never a bad thing, because you will be surprised at what comes out of it. And I think for those of you going through programs now or alumni, like over communicate with us, right, I say to companies all the time that I can try and help you with 100 % of the things that I know about, I can't help you with any of the things that I don't. And so the more that we know in advance that things are going well or badly or otherwise, the more that hopefully we can we can help. I think the other thing I would say is be nimble. So as our business kind of tanks effectively in Ireland and the UK, we had an opportunity to open up an office in Dubai. And I think because we were a little bit smaller, a little bit leaner and looking for kind of opportunities and still obviously very hungry. We took that we started building our own products out there. So iOS and Android travel guides for the Arabic speaking markets, and working with lots and lots of other people out there. And the financial crisis, thankfully, had not quite hit that part of the world quite as much. And through that kind of the think, we not been open to trying things, even in the most difficult circumstances, the outcome would have been very different. But certainly it was, you know, I think, a lesson learned in terms of just taking some opportunities that are in front of you and still being willing to take risks where you've kind of adequately thought about them. So just my two cents worth, know, as also as the saying goes, this will pass, right, I think there have been a number of kind of bumps along the way over the last, you know, couple of decades. And I think this is no different. I think, you know, it's a black swan event. No, you know, no one saw this coming. And it's going to be very challenging. But I think the far side of it, you know, there will be great companies who go through this period and come out on the far side. And I'm hoping that we'll be able to support you through that. So Jenny, hand over to you to share your story.

[SPEAKER_01]
Jenny well, thanks, everyone for joining. I'm seeing so many, you know, friendly faces and names in the chat. It's really awesome. Over, you know, 300 people on the Techstars network are on this. So that's actually making me feel really good, especially because you know, what I really think our strength is at Techstars is being a network. And you know, this is one of the advantages we have over, you know, other other groups is that like, we are really tight knit community, we've got a lot of resources, and we're really here for you. So whether it's the managing directors, you know, people like Casey on the marketing team, like we're all kind of banding together to help. And so you know, to echo, Aamon sentiment, definitely reach out, like be proactive, be communicative with with people here and you know, in the communities that you're part of. So yeah, so I started a company in 2006. I'm kind of an on, you know, an accidental entrepreneur, and that you know, I had a problem that I saw that I was like, passionate about solving, I didn't really know, I didn't even think I'd heard of the term venture capital or really thought about, you know, a scalable startup, you know, versus kind of a small business. So ended up starting a company in 2006. We ended up raising from some angels, and those angels were people that kind of knew us and, and, you know, believed in us as a team. But I don't think we ever, you know, we really weren't thinking about venture. And so we ran it very lean and kind of from the beginning, it was almost like a bootstrap business. We were, we were in the mobile space, in the kind of international telco space, and we were actually making money from day one. So that was helpful. And so we're running the business. And then we start kind of hearing people say, like, you know, you guys should raise money, and you should really build this out. And the kind of like, you know, it got in our head that just like, you know, the only way to grow this was, was to raise capital, which was kind of interesting. So in 2007, I went out to Silicon Valley to try to raise capital, because in New York City, there really wasn't any. And people said, you know, if you're going to scale this, you've got to take money from VCs out west. So we spent about a month out there meeting with investors and, you know, trying to figure out if there was a if there were people that, you know, really believed in in this business, we definitely got, you know, a bunch of interest. And we're kind of in the midst of negotiating term sheets. And, you know, you guys know kind of what happened then, right? So Lehman collapses, and all of a sudden, the world goes into kind of turmoil. And we were really caught off guard. So, you know, I think the, you know, the big learning for me is that, you know,

[None]
obviously,

[SPEAKER_01]
you know, these things are really hard to anticipate. But we had just we we'd done so much planning around growth. We really like, you know, we built our models, we built our metrics, we were always talking about how to build this, you know, in in a massive way, we hadn't really thought about what's worst case scenario, what if we have to go back to bootstrapping? How do we run this business? Oh, my gosh, we have 50 employees. And so we had done no planning. [None]
And so

[SPEAKER_01]
we were selling, you know, we were selling minutes to people that were calling internationally, it actually turned out to be pretty good for our business, because in bad times, people pick up the phone, it turns out, but we had no idea if that was going to be the case. Hi, this is Zibby Owens, and you're listening to Totally Booked with Zibby. Formerly, moms don't have time to read books. Stay in the know, get insider insights, and connect with guests like I do every single day. For more information, go to zibbymedia.com and follow me on Instagram at Zibby Owens. Jenny Fielding is the author of Venture Everywhere, Travel, Entrepreneurship, and a Roadmap for Life. Jenny is a seasoned venture capitalist and technology trailblazer with a diverse background in law, finance, and entrepreneurship. As the founder of Two Tech Startups, she understands the challenges of building companies from the ground up. Now, with a decade of investing experience and a portfolio valued at $10 billion, Jenny leads Everywhere Ventures, the go -to venture fund for early -stage founders around the world. Beyond investing, Jenny is an adjunct professor at Columbia University and Cornell Tech, where she inspires the next generation of entrepreneurs. [SPEAKER_01]
And ladies and gentlemen, next on investing in Asia, please welcome Mr. Nathan Sivaga -Nanathan. Please give him a big round of applause.

[SPEAKER_00]
Good afternoon, everybody. First of all, the name is very long because it's Sri Lankan. And talking about digital systems when I was coming through the airport, the immigration, my name was too long for it to be processed. So it took me 45 minutes to get through the immigration. But my love for Pakistan actually started because Sri Lanka won the World Cup in Lahore. And ever since then, I've had a soft spot for Pakistan. And six months ago, to kind invitation from Shahid, I ended up coming to NDU and started really looking at the opportunities in Pakistan. I think Pakistan is at that crux of making a decision on whether it wants to be a Jamaica or whether it wants to be a Singapore. That choice is really now. And when I was looking at what we do in the venture capital world and looking at where we are in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, I started drawing some parallels. And today's presentation is really identifying where Pakistan should go. Because what we normally do, as humans are, is we look to the West and what's happening in Silicon Valley, what's happening in Europe, and start comparing ourselves to that part of the world. But when we do look at investments, we look at it differently. And I think one of the key things that I want to talk about today is really comparing Southeast Asia and South Asia and the opportunities that arise for Pakistan because of that. A quick thing on Panama. What we do is we focus on mass market around this region. We've been investing for the last 15 years. We have seven offices around the globe. And we're about to sign a partnership today with Seed Ventures in bringing some capital into Pakistan. The opportunities in tech in Pakistan is immense. And when you really look at the population and the opportunities around, you don't have to be shipping goods all around the world. You already have a great STEM education system here. You have 2.5 billion people around Asia. And specifically, over 1.9 billion in South Asia. When you look at something like the SME sectors and you look at the opportunities around that in Pakistan, it's extremely high. And with a young population and a very educated population, and we have many working in AI for us, this opportunity is something that you've got to decide on whether you want to be a Singapore or whether you want to be a Jamaica. ASEAN is the fifth largest economy in the world at $28 trillion. When you look at the incomes that are rising in those areas, and you look at South Asia and the income rising here, there are certain patterns that you start to look at. And one of the patterns that we always look at is the $10,000 threshold. In 2012, China was at $10,000 threshold. And the e -commerce platforms and all of the digital platforms started doing well, including payment systems, WeChat, etc. And what we started noticing in Southeast Asia now is that Southeast Asia is at that point. It's at that $10,000 level point. And when you look at South Asia, it's getting to that point as well. So the purchasing power is increasing. And what we're noticing is 73 % of the people are purchasing something new that they've never purchased before in their life in Southeast Asia. Southeast Asia and South Asia is very resilient as well. When you look at all of the economic crashes, the dot -com crash, etc., the economy still continues to survive. And this is a great indicator as to why that is. Because the population itself is self -sufficient and large enough for it to really conceive itself within that country and really create an economy from the country itself. The other particular reason is that sometimes when you don't have anything, that's the greatest opportunity possible. When landlines were not available and mobile phone technology came, they were able to grow into the mobile phone technology. And every year, that percentage increases. If you look at a 90 million usage increase over the last three years in ASEAN countries, and when you look at the penetration in places like Pakistan, it's very high. But with this high amount of usage, what can you do? And that's what really venture capital we're looking at. How do you bring technology into investment in Southeast Asia? What Indonesian story in the internet economy, 73 % of Indonesians are buying something new every year. On average, they have at least five platforms that they're using in the digital space. And they continue to load new apps all the time because of that. And that means the economy is really moving to that digital world. Yes, you do need bandwidth. Yes, you do need infrastructure. But I think the basic infrastructure that you have, you can get to that place as well. If you look at the countries individually, one in three millennials are in ASEAN. They're a mobile -first economy. The economy will grow by eight times by 2025. Companies in China are moving into these regions because of the growth that's needed and it's bringing cash. Unfortunately, South Asia still lacks that cash. And that's where the opportunity is for us. Electronic payments are on the increase. The methods of payments are on the increase. Alibaba coming into Pakistan is a great indicator of where things are going to lead. What we need to get to is trying to get to this unicorn level of having at least one unicorn come out of Pakistan in the next few years. Whereas in Southeast Asia, the timeline for a unicorn shrunk. So in South Asia, we believe that the timeline for a unicorn will shrink as well. And we should aim towards bringing that one unicorn by 2022. There's also another reason when we look at venture capital in this region is the multiples. The multiples that we are looking at today is in ASEAN region is 13 and a half, 14 times multiples. In this region, we're looking at four to five times multiple. This is the best time to be investing in series A, series B in venture. And that's where the real opportunity is because when you invest at a four times, five times multiple, your returns are in the 28, 30 % range. And that's where you need to deploy your capital. It's not just in private equity, but in growth capital, in venture capital. What we look at as limited partners in our investors is the consistent returns. And what you're seeing in the last three years, the consistent returns have come out of Southeast Asia. They're much higher. And looking at places like India as well. And that, again, is a great opportunity that Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar now has as well. LPs always expect higher returns. And what we're seeing is that over 65 to 70 % of the LP returns are over 22%. So if you invest the dollar today, the idea is that there'll be 22 % return in a very fast period. And that's where I think patient capital in Pakistan is needed by the families as well. So taking all these learnings from Southeast Asia, what can we do in this part of the world? Well, we have a large population. We have an internet penetration of 30%, where there's an opportunity there. And we have a density of population of 300, 300 kilometers. So these are all great indicators. But when you look at the GDP, it's 1,600 on average. And when you look at Pakistan, it's 1,600 as well. So how do we get the GDP and the disposable income levels higher? Well, the predicted rate of growth in the mobile phones is very high. It's in the next five years in South Asia, it's going to have the highest number of mobile phones that are going to be used. Well, most of the technologies that we need to be investing in, whether it's customs, whether it's clearing, whether it's logistics, you need to be focusing in how do you bring technology in everything we do. And I always do this. I love selfies. I'm going to take a selfie with all of you because I think we need to remember this day because I'm telling you that Pakistan is at that point where it can become a different country to what it is today. When you look at the regions and the fastest growing region, Bangladesh, Pakistan are way up there in South Asia levels. The population is one, but also the growth rates are very good as well. Yes, you have had a blip. Yes, you have had a dollar blip. But I think you bottomed out and I think the opportunities for us is now. And that's why we're looking at bringing venture capital into Pakistan. When you also look at the accelerated growth and new consumer focused technologies, there is an increase on GNI per capita in Pakistan as well. But what's missing is money. Money at angel level is there. Money at family level, control level, where they would like to take a large percentage in startup companies in series A and B is there. But global venture capital is still not available in South Asia as an overall plot. When you look at the global economy size and the size of the economies in South Asia and Southeast Asia, the amount of money that's deployed by venture capital is very less. So that's why I think attracting more venture capital into Pakistan is a key focus that this country needs to give and make the regulations simple enough for people to invest. I'm going to skip these next two slides due to lack of time, but I'll get to this one. One of the things that we look at are these other stages that we look at. Can we enter a country easily? Can we develop a good pipeline? Can we screen and do due diligence easily? Can we structure an investment that makes sense for our LPs? And then managing investment and follow ons and exits. There are two areas that Pakistan needs to work on. One is screening and due diligence. It's sometimes very difficult to get data. And the second is exit. We can help with the exit because when we go in packs as venture capitalists, we are able to attract other venture capitalists to come along. And I feel that if you look at a seven -year horizon in Pakistan and invest for the long term between seven and ten years, then there's the opportunity for you to really get good returns in companies and also get good returns in development technology as well. I'm moving on to my final slide and this is the one I want to focus a little bit on. So what does all this mean? Technology, talking about future, you're talking about venture capital. It all boils down to this chart. There are favorable fundamentals today in Pakistan. That is an underserved consumer, large mass market, affordable mobile phones, growing disposable income, and government support and a very young population, including myself.

[None]
But to

[SPEAKER_00]
enable all of this, you need good logistics. In Southeast Asia, they're putting $150 billion into infrastructure. Now that's a lot of money. But their return on that $150 billion is $25 billion a year. This is per annum numbers. So logistics can only be achieved through technology at a cheaper cost. There are so many logistics companies that are around. And the opportunities for other companies like Food Pandas here on the food side, Uber Eats, they're all, I would say, in a very early stage, but that's really serving the consumer. But logistics across the board in terms of truck utilization, in terms of road utilization, in terms of railway utilization, and digitizing those is the greatest opportunity. And we would invest in companies that are looking at bringing synergies in those sectors. EdTech. We've had a lot of learning on this in Vietnam. Forty percent of most people drop out at secondary school. And the opportunity to get a university degree is very less. Here's where technology can help. We've got a company in Vietnam that we invested very early, and it's been able to scale past Vietnam into other countries, including Thailand, and to different age groups as well. But what they've done is gone into universities, helped those university courses be digitized, and made them affordable so that everybody has access to them. Because the number of universities places are very less. And therefore, now, you're bringing affordable education through different forms. And there are many different types of opportunities around EdTech that Pakistan will focus on. FinTech. I don't want to know about mobile wallets. I think that's a done deal. Everybody can do it. It's nothing new. I think FinTech is more about creating business models. It's creating credit. It's creating insurance. It's creating SME and MSME. It's creating savings and payments. The opportunity arises in terms of digitizing some of these areas, and it's actually a FinTech play. We had a company in Indonesia, which we just exited to GoJack, which was working on a very simple method. It was trying to understand the shopkeeper at a rural level, and how they were trying to serve the community. But at the same time, I think here it's called the committee, where people put money together on a monthly basis or a weekly basis, and have a lotto to take the money out. They were using the committee system to really bring product. And I'm trying to understand, why do they collect money? What's the product they want to build? And at one point, they had 250,000 outlets that were really serving the community. Now, that's FinTech in a different way, but FinTech with e -commerce as well. So, now, why did GoJack buy it? GoJack bought it, and it's called GoPay now, because it's a FinTech play. So, it's not just about mobile wallets. And my advice to everybody who's building mobile wallets is, there are other business models that you can solve, and look at those business models, because that's where you will make the biggest impact to the community, and also be able to grow as well. The third area is e -commerce, and the opportunity for e The very high, and I think there are already some platforms that are coming across, and you see a high level of engagement with the millennials on the e -commerce sites. But again, on e -commerce, there are different forms of doing it. We've looked at various different industries, how that can be automated, whether it's pharmaceutical. So, we have in Philippines and in Indonesia, the largest pharmaceutical chain that's connected all the pharmacies in both of these countries, over 200,000 pharmacies that are working both B2B and B2C, in really bringing e -commerce to the consumer at the end. And finally, I'm going to talk a little about health tech, because it's an offline online model. It's a virtual doctor is a key part of that as well. So, how do you bring hardware, which is hospitals, testing, etc. How do you have the best cardiologist who is living in Karachi treat someone who is two hours away? And how do you build those virtual bandwidth within the system to be able to bring edtech? So, these are things I believe that Pakistan has opportunities in. And it's really up to you guys as to whether you want to be a Singapore or whether you want to be a Jamaica. And the time is now. And people in the families that are investing need to get into the venture capital world and start investing in venture capital to really grow these companies to be regional players and not just a country player. Thank you.

We've come a long way from the early days of computing, when computers were enormous machines hidden in back rooms. These machines could only be operated by an elite priesthood who knew the secret languages that computers could understand. It wasn't until the first killer app came along that democratized computing. That killer app? Excel spreadsheets. Excel empowered people to complete complex tasks on a computer without code. And so began the no -code movement. Fast forward to today, and we have a new priesthood. Data scientists typically work in silos within companies and are tasked with mountains of work. But behind the curtain, data scientists spend 80 % of their time on non -revenue generating tasks such as labeling data. We are on the cusp of another Excel spreadsheet moment. My name is Mason. I'm a co -founder and CEO of Swivel. We are no -code for machine learning. Today, every company deploying AI starts by building the same tools from the ground up over and over again. I, personally, have built these tools three times in my entrepreneurial career and have worked with Fortune 1000 companies who have also had this problem. We provide the picks and shovels that help companies build world -class AI algorithms. Every project needs three things to be successful. High -quality training data, simple deployment into a production environment, and a closed feedback loop that ensures the system continually gets smarter. There are companies who do some of these things separately, but Swivel has simplified all these tools into a single platform. No other company controls the entire AI data pipeline. But the real breakthrough is making it as easy as a single button press. We in doing so, shortening the time to implementing AI from an average of six months to six seconds. We started with a focus on natural language. But over the past year, we've expanded from language modeling to audio, and now images, allowing us to expand our impact across a single organization as well as meet the growing needs of the market. We charge a platform fee for accessing our tools, and a volume fee for the amount of annotation work we complete for each customer. In the past two months, we've grown the number of annotations we outsource more than tenfold, helping our customers increase conversions and gross margins, and reduce cost while improving their customers' experience. Just over the last six months, we've doubled annual recurring revenue to over $200,000. And have a working sales pipeline valued at $1.2 million. Our customers include Verizon, JB Hunt, and Extra Space Storage. But today, we have something even more exciting to announce. We've entered into engagements with both Cox Communications and Cox Automotive. Our solution is sitting in the middle of two rapidly growing markets. And 2020 just pushed the fast -forward button on both of them. A third -party data labeling market and a low -code market projected to grow north of $20 billion by 2024. SWIVL's leadership team has been working together since early 2016. And we've exited together. We sold an educational AI platform. So the entire team not only has a deep understanding of the problem space, but we know what it takes to get a company from inception to exit. Today, we're creating another Excel spreadsheet moment. Democratizing AI for every maker within every organization. SWIVL is the single platform that ensures the highest quality training data for your AI project. Over the past six months, we've grown the number of annotations tenfold and doubled our annual recurring revenue. If you're an investor, a company leader looking to speed up your AI workflow, up AI or someone interested in joining a rockstar team, I invite a conversation.
