Hi everyone, super excited to be here. I've been wanting to come up to Montreal for actually years and finally got here. So I'm thrilled. Thank you, Rebecca, for the wonderful invite and it's been incredible being here the last few days. So how many founders in the audience? Hopefully mostly founders put those hands up. Okay, great. How many people are raising capital or have raised capital? All right, a little bit less. Well, I'm gonna save a few minutes for Q &A. So please tee up your questions for the end. I hope that this gonna provide kind of a framework of things to think about in terms of fundraising. It'd be great to have your questions. So the name of the talk is What's Your True North? It's around early stage fundraising, but I could really call the talk maybe venture capital is not right for you. Or supporters in the front row. Or different alternatives to venture capital. So we'll talk a little bit about how to figure out what type of funding is actually right for you. So a little bit about myself. So I come from a family of entrepreneurs, but really small business entrepreneurs. So my grandfather owned fruit stores in Brooklyn. My grandparents were all immigrants. My other grandfather, he was an accountant and, you know, hung his shingle outside his house and, you know, had a practice in the basement. Both my parents worked for themselves. And so the model growing up was really around creating, you know, wealth independently, but really like working for yourself. And figuring out a model that works for you. So that was kind of my model growing up. And despite that, I ended up at really big companies. So I worked at Nike and JP Morgan and kind of learned how to be in that big corporate beast. And at some point, 2006, so pretty early, I left all that to start a startup. Most people thought I was pretty crazy. Most people in my world were working in corporate or other very traditional, traditional places. And, you know, there I was starting a tech company, not as a technical, as a non -technical founder. And so because I'd come from this kind of traditional background of corporate, I was very focused on revenue and profitability. And so our company actually from, you know, pretty much day one, we bootstrapped it and we were actually, you know, doing quite well. We were hitting all the milestones, all of our goals. And we took in a very small amount of venture, or sorry, of not of venture capital. We took in a very small amount of kind of friends and family to help us go. And then, you know, ended up not raising any more capital. So we were hitting all our milestones. Things were looking, you know, pretty good. I made a lot of mistakes along the way, but that's a different talk. And all of a sudden, you know, the business became a little bit unmanageable and I had to figure out what to do with it. I got on an airplane one day. I sat next to this guy. After three hours, he said, I'm going to buy your company. And a few months later, I sold my company. So this slide, success and failure, was really a moment for me where I kind of understood investing in a very different way. So for me, I'd sold my company, I'd made a bunch of money, I was able to buy an apartment, do a lot of things that, you know, that I set out to do. But it was a pretty small, modest exit. I'd only run the company for three years. But it felt like a success to me. The thing was, this company would have been a massive failure to most of the VCs that I know, right? Didn't turn into a billion dollar company. And I would go out to California and people would be like, oh, yeah, you worked really hard on that company, Jenny. Too bad it didn't work out. And I was like, hmm, interesting. Like my, you know, everyone in my company had like this great job. And, you know, it had afforded me kind of all this freedom. I was taking a year off and yet like I was a failure to some people and to some people I was a success. So I was like trying to kind of understand this. And I realized, you know, that that dichotomy, a lot of that is just not really understanding, you know, when to take the right capital at the right time. And so kind of fast forward to today where I really consider myself, you know, less of an investor and more as a mentor and a coach to startups who all come and pitch me. I've invested in about 130 companies and these things come up time and time again of are you pitching the right deal to the right investor? So I kind of came up with this framework of like, what's your true north? And so the first thing I do is when I meet a founder, as I sit down with them and I really try to understand what type of business do you want to build? Do you want to build a massive billion dollar business? Do you want to build a lifestyle business? And there's lots in between. And the truth is there's really no right answer, but it is a moment of introspection for you to figure out what type of company you actually want to build, because that will help you figure out what type of capital is right for you. So I'm just going to very quickly go through some options and then again at the end, love to take some of your questions. So a lifestyle business that was, you know, the fruit stores in Brooklyn, right? So that was a small business, you know, potentially you could maybe get a loan for that, but, you know, really focused on something that was modest. And I think, you know, today there's, you know, if you say that you're building a lifestyle business, maybe more of a services type business in the tech world, people kind of look down on you. But that's actually, you know, if you look at the US, like the US was built on small businesses, right? And so it is something to celebrate, but I feel like in the tech world, we've kind of decided small businesses are not great businesses. [SPEAKER_00]
Welcome to the Startup of the Year podcast, where each episode we showcase exciting new companies from around the world. This podcast is produced by Established, creators of the Startup of the Year program. Established is focused on helping organizations with their innovation, startup, and communication strategies.

[SPEAKER_02]
Hello, welcome back to the Startup of Year podcast. I'm Frank Ruber, your host. I'm also the co -CEO of Established and managing partner at Established Ventures. I'm excited today to have my guest here. She's a pioneer investor, entrepreneur, and an author of a new book, Venture Everywhere. And her name is Jenny Feeling. And she's the co -founder and managing partner of Everywhere Ventures and an early stage investor backing global founders all over the world. She's formerly the managing director at Techstars, where she mentored and invested in lots of companies, hundreds probably, as well as started her own two companies, two mobile software startups, and then eventually moved over to Venture. So welcome, Jenny. Thanks so much for being here and excited to have you on the show.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thanks for having me, Frank. I feel like you and I go way back. So it's always fun to see you again.

[SPEAKER_02]
Absolutely. I appreciate doing it. And yeah, it's been a while since we last caught up, but I'm excited about your book. It's really, you know, easy read. And you can get these like little vignettes you can kind of jump in and out of. So I really enjoyed that. But I love how you weave your story of just your background. So let's start with the book because it's front of mind for me. Your book, know, Venture Everywhere, it focuses on global entrepreneurship and, you shares your inspiration in writing it, you know, kind of in the book. So I wanted you to kind of like share some of that a little bit. You don't have tell all the whole story, like, you know, leave a little bit for folks to go get the book, but a little bit of inspiration of what, you know, what you brought, why you brought this to the world and, you know, what you want readers to get out of it.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah. So as you mentioned, the book is about global entrepreneurship and really what we can all learn from founders building companies around the world and all, you know, far from the globe, Sucum Valley. So I interview founders, you know, in multiple continents and multiple countries. And I, as I interviewed these entrepreneurs and really, as I've met these entrepreneurs over the last 10 to 15 years of traveling to over a hundred companies, I noticed some common themes and through lines in their stories and that have affected and really, you know, influence their perspective on how they see the world and how they've built their companies and how they live their life. So in the book, I call it the everywhere mindset and I kind of break down some of the principles, but really the book is about, you know, having the courage to chart your own path. And so you kind of asked about the inspiration. The book starts with me visiting my grandparents in Brooklyn and hearing my grandmother just going on this trip to Europe. And I convinced, you know, her and our family that I should go with her for like months, you know, on this like crazy journey. My grandmother was very eccentric, but she was a real influence on me and my grandparents who were all kind of entrepreneurs and not tech entrepreneurs, but, you know, people that had forged their own businesses. My grandfather owned fruit stores throughout Brooklyn and just seeing kind of the resilience that you need to build a business and, you know, just the lifestyle that they had, but then also kind of the freedom that they had was very inspirational for me. What's funny is that I kind of went the opposite way. I very traditionally went to law school, I worked in finance. And then when I finally had the guts to start a company, I think I reflected back on just that kind of that nature of, you know, many people in my family who had decided to, you know, become entrepreneurs, maybe sometimes out of necessity. So, so yeah, it was fun. It's a very personal, very personal book. You learn a lot about me, but really, you know, the message is around, you know, the, the incredible entrepreneurs who are just building, you know, massive companies around the world.

[SPEAKER_02]
I love that about this book. You really do share a lot and I think it helps, you know, connect better with you, but also connect better with the reader and share the stories that you're, you're, you're sharing. I love the stories about your grandparents too. I thought they

[None]
were great.

[SPEAKER_02]
And so let's, let's rewind a second though. You talked about the everywhere mindset. Can you just explain that a little bit more and like how founders can develop it?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, I think sometimes, you know, when we grow up in the States or we grow up, you know, in, around Silicon Valley, we can be very, you know, US centric or we kind of see, you know, things just unfold for us. And I think in the world that we live in, especially right now, this kind of volatile world, we have to all, you know, develop these, you know, some of the, these characteristics that help us get through our day and build our companies. So I talk about things like building conviction and how do you do that, especially when the world is against you or a fun one of the everywhere mindset is this idea of moxie, which in many cultures, you know, is just not looked upon favorably, right? It's like having that chip on your shoulder, being a little salty, but the truth is like, you know, some of the best entrepreneurs that is, they've had to develop that or they have that. And I think there's stuff that we can all learn from those people. We don't, you know, even in the US, we're kind of taught, like, you need to be liked and you need to, and I'm trying to break some of those things down and say, like, we're much more complex than that, right? Like, sure, you need to, you know, you need to be able to get along with people and be in the world. But like being liked may not be the characteristics that's going to drive your business, your career, your life to success. And so let's, you know, kind of look at the other side of some of these characteristics.

[SPEAKER_02]
Absolutely. And there's certain, like you said, certain regions that Moxie is just built in inherently, like, they just have this, this swagger, you know, about how they go about things and don't, you know, not giving up. So definitely seen it as well. And wanted to talk a little bit more about maybe, you know, you know, we're talking about a lot of places outside of Silicon Valley. What are some of the biggest misconceptions about launching a startup outside of one of the, you know, major tech hubs, Silicon Valley, Boston, New York, that you've seen?

[None]
Yeah, I

[SPEAKER_01]

We saw that with cryptocurrency, especially with some of the harsh regulations in the US, you know, until more recently, that the best cryptocurrency companies were building in Singapore, they were building in Switzerland, they weren't building here. We also just saw kind of the distribution of cash, right? And that, you know, developing ecosystems, whether they're in the US or elsewhere, we're starting to attract cash and that people in those ecosystems who, you know, have made money have started to think about, you know, the next generation and supporting that generation. So I think it just takes a long time to develop that, you know, that next generation and that mindset of like, hey, I want to, you know, help out, you know, the next innovators. And so we really started to see that in places like New York, when I started my company in 2007, it was a pretty grim place to run a company. And now you think, wow, second largest ecosystem. It's so amazing. It took a long time to develop. So what's cool about, you know, the book and some of these locations is these didn't happen overnight. So, you know, I profile a founder in Brazil and one in Mexico and one, you know, in Nigeria. Like it took a long time for these ecosystems to come about, but it's a very exciting moment as, you know, capital starts, you know, really flowing in those places.

[SPEAKER_02]

[None]
hubs. I mean, people

[SPEAKER_01]

[None]
material here.

[SPEAKER_01]
We have a lot of capital. It's not venture capital, but we have, you know, hella rich people and we have Wall Street and we have real estate. And sure, I'll fly out to Silicon Valley and make sure that I'm like well networked, but I'm going to build my company here. And so now we're just seeing that, you know, all over the world, which is super cool. [SPEAKER_02]
Yeah, I agree. And, you know, it's taken, what, almost 20 years, I feel like, to get to that point. But it's really fun to watch it evolve. And, you know, you shared some success stories, you mentioned a couple places a moment ago. Can you share like one success story that kind of embodies the whole everywhere philosophy? Like one that sticks out the most? You're like, this is like the perfect poster

[None]
job. Yeah,

[SPEAKER_01]
I mean, there's so many. But one of the stories I love is an entrepreneur who grew up in a small town in Pakistan. And, you know, his family, you know, had not been educated. And they run like a small shop, you know, in their town. But they always wanted their children to kind of have a better life. We hear this story all the time. So the founder at the age of, I don't know, like 16 or 17 gets a scholarship to UCLA. Like he's never even left his town, never been on an airplane and shows up in Los Angeles. Right. And so, you know, just imagine that cultural, I mean, crazy. But he really thrives and he makes friends and he, you know, just like puts himself out there. He has some setbacks. But, you know, fast forward, that founder ends up moving, you know, to the Middle East. And he starts a company called Kareem. And like think about where he came from and what the drive was to succeed and what it was like to come to the U.S., you know, at that moment. And just, you know, such a different experience. So I love highlighting those founders who are not scared to get on a plane, who are not scared to interact with other cultures, which is a really, you know, part of the theme of the book. It's really about having empathy and awareness for other cultures and realizing that the world is increasingly more interconnected. Now, these founders that I profile in the book, they learn that out of necessity. Many have to flee their war -torn countries or countries that don't have a lot of resources. So for them, it's necessity. And I think for folks in the U.S., many of the people reading the book, there's a lot we can all learn from that, especially in this moment, which is a kind of interesting moment in U.S. history.

[SPEAKER_02]

I'm saying, look back, like, you know, maybe 20 years ago, if you were working at a company, you know, maybe you were working mostly with people in the U.S. or maybe in your town or city, I mean, what company right now doesn't have international clients that you need to interact with or people on your team that are in other countries? And if you can't develop the skill set to interact with them and understand, like, that's just such a fundamental skill that maybe you didn't need all those years ago. So, you know, I'm taking an opposite stance, which, like, we're living in a global world. You know, when we meet founders, many of them are thinking about global markets. They're not just thinking about, you know, selling into one place. And I think, you know, we need to change our DNA in the U.S. and really kind of think about, you know, what that means to be global. So, yeah, I'm taking a very opposite stance to what you're hearing. And I just think that reflects the lives that, you know, that we live and the technologies that we use and the people that we interact with. It's just very different than it was before.

[SPEAKER_02]

[None]

[SPEAKER_00]
Each chapter of Venture Everywhere lands in a particular geographical area and covers my experiences and stories in that place, both personal and professional, and, at times, comical. I also describe the business and startup culture there, sharing insights and context. The individual chapters will also have a companion founder profile, related in some way to the geographical area I explore in the core of the chapter. Each profile will be underpinned by one of the six characteristics of the Everywhere mindset and demonstrate how the founder used it to be successful in their work, as well as how that trait can be cultivated and nurtured more broadly. This isn't a typical business book with formal lessons, but whether you're an entrepreneur, investor, career switcher, or travel enthusiast, you'll benefit from the concepts within. The founders I interview originate in what many consider far -flung places, ranging from Brazil to Barcelona, Saudi Arabia to the Philippines, and everywhere in between. Learning about, and, often, investing in and working with these inspirational people, has revealed to me the secret they've unlocked about how the world works, and that's having an everywhere mindset. Through that concept, Venture Everywhere will help people develop business, life, and interpersonal skills, all wrapped up in my entertaining travelogue, highlighting the aspects of the cultures and places I find truly fascinating. Ultimately, it's not about simply sending your kids to Mandarin class or memorizing capital cities on a map. It's about having empathy and awareness for other cultures and realizing the world is increasingly more interconnected. At almost any company, or in any role, people will have intercultural experiences through team members, leaders, and customers. And now, with the rise of distributed teams, every company is relying on global talent. Showing openness and being comfortable working in these diverse and context -switching environments is a necessary skill that bestows a competitive edge in today's business environment. Showing than anything, though, Venture Everywhere is a permission slip for the person who wants to live, travel, build, and experience all life has to offer. You don't have to be born in Silicon Valley to be a great entrepreneur. And, you don't need what you might think you need to build a career or business, grow or evolve in your career, or stay relevant. You don't have to play by the rules and live in one place. Success doesn't mean 20 years at a huge corporation and a gold watch upon retirement. It means charting your own path. I'm offering my listeners the inspiration and the liberation to become global citizens and creators, free from bygone societal expectations and norms. For those of us in the know, it's a new playbook for how to live.

Venture Everywhere

In this special episode of Venture Everywhere, co-founders and Managing Partners of Everywhere Ventures, Jenny Fielding and Scott Hartley, turn the tables, as Scott interviews Jenny about her new book, Venture Everywhere. Building companies outside traditional hubs.

Venture Everywhere with Jenny Fielding
Lifeselfmastery's podcast I Startups I Venture Capital
39 min
Jenny Fielding is the co-founder and Managing Partner of Everywhere Ventures. She is the author of the book, Venture Everywhere
In this episode, Jenny Fielding, co-founder and managing partner of Everywhere Ventures, shares her journey from corporate law and startup founder to becoming a top pre-seed investor. She discusses the transition from running startups to venture capital, the challenges of building a micro-fund, and the power of community-driven investing. She also talks about her book Venture Everywhere, highlighting inspiring founders worldwide, and much more!

Jenny Fielding - Venture Everywhere - Jenny Fielding on AI Start Ups, Ethical Innovation and the Future of Founders
Redefining AI: Leadership, Ethics and the Future of Artificial Intelligence
22 min
After winning the prestigious New York Digital Award in 2024, Redefining AI returns with an electrifying Season Four!
Join your host Lauren Hawker Zafer, on behalf of Squirro, the Enterprise Gen AI Platform, as we embark on another season of groundbreaking conversations.
In this episode of Redefining AI, host Lauren Hawker Zafer sits down with Jenny Fielding: investor, founder, operator, professor, and author of Venture Everywhere.
With a career that spans over 300 startup investments, including fintech, healthtech, and edtech disruptors like Alloy, Particle Health, and Pair Eyewear, Jenny offers rare insights into the future of AI startups, founder-first investing, and the changing landscape of early-stage tech innovation.
Together, they explore:
What separates AI hype from real-world investable opportunities
How to build ethical, responsible AI startups
The rise of founder-market fit in the age of GenAI tools
Navigating trust, regulation, and scale in sectors like fintech, healthcare, and education
How Gen Z entrepreneurs are rethinking AI and purpose
What it truly takes to build a scalable and meaningful AI company
Jenny also shares lessons from Columbia and Cornell Tech, her thoughts on democratizing entrepreneurship globally, and why her book Venture Everywhere is a call to action for responsible innovation.
Whether you're a tech founder, investor, or simply curious about the future of AI entrepreneurship, this conversation offers clarity, candor, and bold ideas for building what matters.
🎧 Tune in now and explore how AI, venture capital, and human-centric design are redefining the next wave of innovation.

Venture Everywhere: Jenny Fielding on Backing 300+ Startups, Building a $10B Portfolio & Redefining Global VC
What does it take to back over 300 startups, build a $10 billion portfolio, and launch one of the most dynamic global venture funds?
In this energising episode of Authentic Achievements, host Kim-Adele Randall welcomes Jenny Fielding — one of the world’s most active early-stage investors, co-founder of Everywhere Ventures, and author of the new book Venture Everywhere. Jenny’s career spans corporate law, tech entrepreneurship, and top-tier venture capital — and her journey is nothing short of extraordinary.
Jenny shares behind-the-scenes insights from her path to building a global investment network, what she looks for in standout founders, and why adopting an "everywhere mindset" is key to thriving in the future of entrepreneurship.
🔑 What You’ll Learn:
📖 The story behind Jenny’s new book Venture Everywhere
👩‍⚖️ How she transitioned from corporate law to tech startups to leading global VC
💥 The reality of launching a venture fund in uncertain markets
💡 What truly differentiates exceptional founders and startups today
🌍 Why geographic flexibility and mindset diversity are the future of venture capital
👤 About Jenny Fielding:
Jenny Fielding is a globally recognised early-stage investor and co-founder of Everywhere Ventures. She’s backed over 300 startups, built a $10B portfolio, and helped shape the next generation of tech leaders. Formerly Managing Director at Techstars, Jenny is also a sought-after speaker and newly published author. Her work empowers founders around the world to succeed—wherever they are.

Beyond Vibe Testing: Smarter Eval for Agentic AI
In this episode of Inference Time Tactics, Rob, Cooper, and Byron explore Salesforce’s CRMArena-Pro benchmark and what it reveals about the limits of enterprise AI agents. They share why benchmark scores often fail in production, how inference-time tactics like best-of-N can improve reliability, and what NeuroMetric is building to make eval easier—from an ITC Test Engine to a drag-and-drop interface for rapid visualization and experimentation. We talked about: Why Salesforce’s CRMArena-Pro benchmark highlights the gap between lab benchmarks and real-world agent reliability. How leading models perform inconsistently across single-turn and multi-turn enterprise tasks. Why benchmark scores are weak predictors of operational success in production. The role of inference-time tactics in reducing variance and improving stability. NeuroMetric’s new platform: ITC Test Engine and drag-and-drop interface for experimentation. Challenges in building agentic systems, from database integration to managing multi-prompt complexity. Why large language models’ stochastic nature conflicts with business demands for reliability. Latency, cost, and rate limits as major bottlenecks in scaling agentic workflows. The limits of “vibe testing” and why rigorous evaluation frameworks are essential. How Google’s Stacks tool speeds up evaluation with LLM-as-judge, and why it still falls short for enterprise needs. AI in ABA: What's Real, What's Noise, and How to Tell
Welcome to another episode of The Flychain Reaction! Every practice owner is getting pitched a new AI tool every other week. Almost none of those conversations happen with someone who has actually run a clinic. Adam Ventura is a BCBA who spent 22 years in behavior analysis, built and ran a multi-state ABA company for nearly a decade, sold it, and then went and built the AI tools he wished he'd had. He's now founder and CEO of Intraverbal AI. Ethan, CEO of Flychain, and Adam get into why AI in ABA should mean augmented intelligence rather than artificial — and why owners who bolt powerful technology onto broken workflows just end up automating the broken workflow faster. Adam shares the concrete red flags and green flags to look for when a vendor pitches you, including the PHI and training-data questions most buyers never think to ask. He also walks through the numbers behind Intraverbal's assessment tool: 340 BCBAs reported spending 18–20 hours on an initial assessment they were only authorized 8–10 hours for, and got it down to 3–4. Along the way: the $3,000 phone call that taught Adam about entity structure, why he thinks education is shifting from teaching the right answers to teaching the right questions, and why specialized data beats a general-purpose model every time.

From Tokenmaxxing to Tokenminning: The Case for Token Engineering
In this episode, Cooper sits down with Neurometric CEO, Rob May, to talk through a big-news month: the show's rebrand from Inference Time Tactics to Token Engineering, the launch of tokenminning.com as a response to the "tokenmaxxing" trend, Neurometric's new token engineering platform and fundraising announcement. But the bigger conversation is about why Rob thinks "token engineering" is about to become a discipline every AI company needs—the same way DevOps or UX became non-negotiable roles—and why he's betting the company on getting there first. We talked about: The origin of tokenminning.com—started as an April Fools' joke and Reddit group—and why it caught fire as a real counterpoint to "tokenmaxxing." Specialized, fine-tuned models beat frontier models on individual tasks. New token engineering platform unifies fine-tuning, distillation, and caching in one system. COGS vs. OPEX: how Neurometric spots which customers feel AI costs most. Integrating with Harbor to run 15,000 agentic evaluation tasks across models like Gemma, Qwen, Mistral, and Granite. Token engineering is becoming a C-suite responsibility, not just an engineering one. THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION

Author’s
Note
SECTION 1

5
The Past - 2024 
In the Big Book of VC - 2024 Annual version report, I wrote that the 
venture market was telling a familiar but important story: cautious 
capital, rising AI influence, and a recovery that never fully arrived. 
Despite strong public markets, venture remained constrained by macro 
uncertainty, weak exits, and muted investment activity—leaving the asset class 
out of sync with broader equities. Fundraising declined globally, with early-
stage activity bearing the brunt, while late stage proved more resilient. The 
U.S. held up better than other regions, driven by large rounds and 
expanding hubs. Across markets, dealmaking became selective, with capital 
flowing disproportionately to a small set of high-conviction opportunities. 
AI continued to reshape venture dynamics, attracting an outsized share of 
funding and accelerating outcomes for a narrow group of winners. Valuations 
recovered unevenly and remained concentrated at the top. Exits remained 
the weakest link. IPO and M&A activity stayed subdued, with limited 
liquidity reinforcing LP caution and slowing capital recycling. Fundraising 
consolidated around fewer, larger platforms, leaving smaller managers under 
pressure despite elevated dry powder across the system. In short, 2024 was 
a year of stabilization without renewal. The market avoided further 
deterioration but failed to reset meaningfully—placing renewed hope, and 
heightened expectations, on a more decisive recovery in 2025. 
Author’s Note: The Past, The Present, and The Future
SECTION - AUTHOR’S NOTE
The Present - 2025 
In the Big Book of VC Q3 report, I wrote, “Momentum Is Building — and 
Broadening!” After a hesitant start to the year, startup fundraising activity was 
clearly moving again, even if the system remains cautious and uneven. This is 
not a full-cycle recovery, but it is a meaningful step forward from the 
post-2022 reset. The rebound is highly concentrated. A small group of AI-
driven companies and well-capitalized firms are doing the heavy lifting, while 
much of the market continues to operate carefully. Strip out the outliers and 
the recovery looks fragile, but real.  
Exits have provided the clearest signs of life. M&A activity has picked up 
meaningfully, IPOs have reopened—selectively—and secondaries have 
become a critical liquidity bridge. AI sits at the center of all three, shaping 
both capital formation and capital return. 
Alongside, the venture business itself remains under pressure. Fundraising is 
slow, LPs are cautious, and capital is deploying unevenly despite ample dry 
powder. Teams are leaner, experience is being rewarded, and efficiency has 
replaced growth-at-all-costs as the dominant operating principle. In short, 
venture isn’t back to full strength, but it’s no longer stalled. The engine 
is running, the wheel is turning, and momentum is returning with 
discipline. After the past few years, that alone is real progress. 
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION

6
SECTION - AUTHOR’S NOTE
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION
The Future - What I’ll Be Watching in 2026? 
So let me explain here again:  
At the end of 2024 we were talking about: “the venture market tells a 
familiar but important story: cautious capital, rising AI influence, and a 
recovery that never fully arrived. In short, 2024 was a year of stabilization 
without renewal. The market avoided further deterioration but failed to reset 
meaningfully—placing renewed hope, and heightened expectations, on a 
more decisive recovery in 2025”  
Then by the end of Q3 2025 we were talking about: “Momentum Is 
Building — and Broadening! In short, venture isn’t back to full strength, but it’s 
no longer stalled. The engine is running, the wheel is turning, and momentum 
is returning with discipline. After the past few years, that alone is real 
progress.” 
In short the expectations from 2024 were largely fulfilled! 
Looking ahead to 2026, I’m focused on five key trends: 
  
VC Fundraising Shock : Of all my projections, this is where I missed most. I 
did not expect VC fundraising to fall as sharply as it has. While the data is 
still partial (only until Q3) and open to debate, the magnitude of the decline 
was surprising. It raises an important question: why did this happen? Low DPI 
is the obvious explanation, yet exits and investment activity have improved this 
year and point to a more constructive outlook for 2026. Against that 
backdrop—especially with public equities near peaks—it’s not immediately 
clear why LP allocations failed to at least match 2024 levels. Lookout for 
revival in 2026 - hopefully
🤞! 
Exits, but Varied : Strong performance from high-profile IPOs in the U.S. 
and India in 2025, coupled with a growing backlog of IPO-ready companies, 
points to meaningful supply build-up that could carry momentum into 2026. 
That said, this should not be taken for granted—macro remains the hardest 
variable to predict, as evidenced by the unexpected Q1 volatility driven by 
shifting trade narratives. Down-round IPOs and post-IPO performance were a 
talking point in 2025 and remain so in 2026. Still, the area I’m most 
constructive on is M&A. Strategic buyers and PE sponsors alike are well-
capitalized and could be looking to deploy dry powder into fitting assets. 
While M&A is not necessarily easier, it is often less directly exposed to macro 
volatility. With U.S. M&A activity already rebounding, the key question is 

7
whether this momentum extends to other markets in 2026. Secondaries have 
also emerged as a vital release valve, and their role as a liquidity bridge is 
set to expand further within the venture ecosystem next year. 
Redefining Seed : Seed investing is at an inflection point. Competition has 
intensified, the number of funds has grown, and megafunds have pushed 
aggressively into the stage. The market is increasingly bifurcated—AI-native 
startups attracting capital at scale, while non-AI companies lag. Traditional 
seed is being squeezed from both ends: pre-seed is encroaching upward, 
while “seed” rounds of $50M+ blur the definition of the stage entirely. 
Smaller funds are struggling to support follow-on rounds, larger seed funds 
are harder to raise, and LPs are actively reassessing seed exposure amid high 
valuations and lower deal volumes. These forces don’t neatly reconcile—
creating exactly the conditions needed to redefine what seed investing 
actually means. 
Late-Stage Renaissance : Late-stage venture reopened in 2025, with deal 
activity and capital deployment picking up—accelerated by strong demand 
for AI leaders. After being the hardest hit in the downturn, late stage is finally 
back in motion, with significant dry powder seeking deployment. That said, 
expectations remain uneven: outside the U.S., many markets still anticipate a 
late-stage capital gap, prompting sovereign LPs to actively support this 
segment. 
SECTION - AUTHOR’S NOTE
The message is clear—the system needs the wheel to keep turning, and it is. 
But this will be a tale of two cities: clear winners attracting capital at scale, 
and a harsh reckoning for those that fail to meet the increasingly high bar on 
growth, quality, and AI relevance. Caution is warranted—but so is optimism. 
Weakness from Within : In Q4, the dominant question has become: Is AI a 
bubble? History suggests that not all bubbles end the same way—some 
unwind quietly, while others permanently reshape markets, even as they 
destroy capital along the way. AI already wields outsized influence through 
infrastructure spending, capex cycles, and its central role in startup growth 
narratives. The key uncertainty lies in how this resolves: life as normal in 
2026, or a sharp correction, or a prolonged monetization lag. Time will tell! 
Best wishes for the holiday season, and here’s to a great start to the New Year!
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION
Rohit Yadav 
Author - The Big Book of VC, Rethinking Venture Capital

Absolutely bullish on the Seed investing space in India, especially in the three 
sectors we invest in as Multiply Ventures- Consumer Brand, Consumer Tech and 
Fintech. The why: Consumption accounts for 60% of India's GDP, and this will 
drive the next decade and beyond. The quality of founders has improved by 
leaps and bounds, and it will only get better. Exits have been an Achilles' heel in 
India, but this changed in 2025 with a remarkable number of IPOs, the launch of 
many secondaries-focused funds, and healthy M&A activity in the consumer 
brand space. Most importantly, a massive social change has been a country-wide 
belief that our time has come, and we can make globally loved products, and we 
like to ﬂaunt them.  
Pattern matching and chasing pedigree founders remains a challenge for the 
industry. Personally curious to watch and learn from the impact of AI on the VC 
industry.
10
Europe’s startup landscape is undergoing a profound shift. Seed funding 
plummeted dramatically in the ﬁrst quarter of 2025 — down 41 percent year over 
year. What may look like a setback is, in fact, a sign of structural 
transformation. Investors are writing larger tickets, but deploying them across 
fewer companies. At the same time, ultra-lean, AI-native startups are increasingly 
skipping the seed stage altogether.  
As a result, today’s seed rounds resemble Series A ﬁnancings from a decade 
ago. Average round sizes have doubled: where seed rounds once ranged between 
one and two million euros, they now frequently land between three and ﬁve 
million euros.  
But this shift also rewrites the rules for founders. Those seeking capital today 
must do far more than simply present a product — they must demonstrate from 
day one that they are building a scalable, high-growth company.
“ “
Predictions for 2026 from Investors and Experts
SECTION - EXPERT VIEWS
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION
Valerie Bures 
Managing Director & Partner 
XAnge
Sanjay Ramakrishnan 
Founder & General Partner  
Multiply Ventures

In 2026, I expect the European early-stage ecosystem to ﬁnd its rhythm again 
after two years of recalibration. Valuations will remain disciplined, but the best 
technical founder, especially in applied AI, climate infrastructure, and industrial 
automation, will command meaningful premiums as their businesses begin to show 
real operating leverage. Fundraising dynamics will stay bifurcated: strong teams 
with capital-efficient traction will close rounds quickly, while everyone else faces 
longer diligence cycles and structured terms.  
On the venture side, LPs will continue prioritizing managers who 
demonstrate clear portfolio construction discipline and tangible DPI rather 
than just paper marks. As a result, VC fund management becomes more 
operationally rigorous, and emerging managers will differentiate through sharper 
theses and tighter ownership strategies. Overall, 2026 won’t be a return to the 
exuberance of past cycles, but it will mark the start of a more durable, 
fundamentals-driven era for startups and venture capital. 
11
2026 will be the year venture ﬁnally separates sourcing from selection. With 
AI democratizing deal discovery and more than 4,000 seed funds now competing 
for the same opportunities, access is no longer an advantage—it’s a commodity.  
Seed valuations remain elevated, multistage ﬁrms continue to push earlier, 
and LPs are becoming far more selective. In this environment, the differentiator 
isn’t who sees a deal ﬁrst, but who truly understands the founder. The strongest 
founders in 2026 will come from unconventional backgrounds and bring a lived, 
earned connection to the problem they’re solving—something no algorithm can 
replicate. As traction becomes easier to manufacture and pedigree becomes 
less predictive, founder–problem ﬁt emerges as the most reliable signal of 
long-term value creation. The next era of venture will reward ﬁrms with depth, 
not breadth, and judgment, not velocity.
“ “
SECTION - EXPERT VIEWS
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION
Sagar Barvaliya 
General Partner 
Blockchain Founders Capital
Oliver Oster 
Founding Partner  
AQVC

Liquidity is the new power line running through the venture ecosystem. In Canada 
and across North America, it has become the deﬁning pressure point for LPs, 
founders and GPs. LPs want ﬂexibility, faster recycling and a clear clock on time 
to liquidity. That alone is reshaping underwriting, governance and how capital 
shows up in early rounds.  
The real shift is happening at pre-seed where angels and early investors are 
expecting more optionality. Instruments that provide a clear path to conversion 
or liquidity are gaining momentum. Structured secondaries and intentional 
liquidity windows are now design choices that can be made on day one. At the 
same time a new architecture is forming. Vertical venture studios engineered for 
real exit pathways. Venture studio funds that treat liquidity as a product 
feature rather than a distant outcome. The next era of venture will reward 
builders who solve liquidity in real time while creating compounding value, not 
those who wait for the market to rescue them.
12
The next wave of breakout companies will be anchored in proximity to 
science, where execution- not hype - drives outsized returns. Translational 
clarity is now the deﬁning edge: clear mechanistic rationale, ﬁt-for-purpose 
biomarkers, and disciplined regulatory plans are narrowing the valley of death for 
teams that know how to build.  
In biosciences, this favors companies that design programs to de-risk early, 
align biology with clinical endpoints, and treat development strategy as a core 
competency rather than an afterthought. These companies tend to move faster 
with fewer surprises and create real option value earlier in their lifecycle. Venture 
is becoming more specialized as a result, with advantage shifting to investors who 
can underwrite true technical inﬂection - biological, clinical, or regulatory - and 
to funds led by investors with real domain ﬂuency, translational depth, and 
operator experience. As the market matures, domain depth and execution 
discipline will quietly outperform generalist approaches. 
“ “
SECTION - EXPERT VIEWS
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION
Megha Unhelkar 
Director of Investments 
Connecticut Innovations
Marcus Daniels 
Founding Partner & CEO  
Highline Beta

Market Liquidity: I don’t see a massive IPO 
window in 2026, yet. However, SME and mid-
market M&A activity is picking up. Secondaries 
are also rising as early investors seek liquidity; for 
the ﬁrst time, secondary volumes exceeded IPO 
volumes. I believe this trend will continue in 2026, 
while VC fundraising hit a 12-year low in 2025 
(down 60% year over year).  
Vibe Coding: Vibe coding is dead, long live vibe 
coding. After massive growth, AI coding traffic 
dropped by 76% globally in recent weeks 
(including Lovable, Base44, Cursor, etc.) as AI 
coding hit its natural limitations. 2026 will reveal 
the overall potential of vibe coding for startups 
and beyond.
13
Outlook for European Early Stage B2B 
Software 
Valuation Dynamics: I expect only gentle upward 
pressure at the pre-seed/seed level, as VCs remain 
disciplined (excluding temporarily hyped topics or 
verticals). More interesting is the high density of 
bootstrapped pre-seed companies raising rounds 
with seed-level metrics and performance.  
Fundraising & Deals: We will see fewer but 
larger pre-seed/seed rounds in 2026 (European 
median (pre-)seed checks jumped ~23% this year). 
Many founders are stitching together bridge 
extensions or raising larger initial rounds to 
extend runway, paired with high capital efficiency 
and swift revenue growth.  
“
The UK has all the fundamental venture 
support for DeepTech (ARIA, Sovereign AI Fund, 
NSSIF, British Business Bank, R&D excellence). 
With entry price and talent arbitrage versus the 
US, the UK and London is the place to build and 
de-risk DeepTech in 2026.
“
SECTION - EXPERT VIEWS
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION
Marc Penkala 
General Partner 
āltitude
Johnathan Matlock 
Co-Founder  
Empirical Ventures 

In 2026, code is commoditized, and the real 
moat is lived experience—not pedigree. 
Operators who’ve lived the customer problem are 
closing rounds faster than Ivy League teams 
because their insights are rooted in reality.  
Monomaniacally obsessed outsider founders—
who’ve absorbed ‘no’ faster—are out-executing 
everyone else, and investors are paying attention. 
In this new cycle, judgment and resilience are the 
only performance metrics that matter. 
14
“
We’re living through a profound shift in the 
startup landscape, away from digital optimisation 
towards Deep Tech innovation built on scientiﬁc 
and engineering breakthroughs. We expect the 
next decade of venture to be de ﬁned by 
breakthroughs in frontier domains such as 
energy, biology, materials, and compute.  
These opportunities resist established venture 
playbooks. Deep Tech founders must convert novel 
primitives into products through path-dependent 
experimentation. Even companies in the same 
vertical often follow radically di fferent 
development trajectories. This is why early-stage 
Deep Tech disproportionately rewards small, 
specialist funds. Immersed in their niche 
ecosystems, these managers understand technical
“
risk, move fast, and provide support that 
generalist ﬁrms cannot.  
But for LPs, a market dominated by specialist 
funds creates friction: high fragmentation, 
smaller ticket capacities, and increased 
underwriting burden. The reality is increased 
concentration into megafunds. While such funds 
are direly needed in later rounds, their incentive 
structure is misaligned with Deep Tech innovation 
at the earliest stages. To avoid this mismatch, the 
industry needs structural innovation in capital 
formation. We expect specialist fund-of-funds 
to gain traction as critical bridges that reduce 
friction for LPs while channeling capital toward 
the specialist managers best equipped to back the 
next generation of breakthrough companies.
SECTION - EXPERT VIEWS
THE BIG BOOK OF VENTURE CAPITAL - 2025 ANNUAL EDITION
Dr. Georg (Juri) Stricker 
General Partner  
Signature Ventures
Joseph Alalou 
Co-Founder & General Partner  
Daring Ventures

Emerging GPs have been trounced since the 
2022 reset, but 2026 is when the best of them 
bounce back. If LPs want to capture the juiciest 
opportunities in this cycle, they can’t just chase 
brands or vintage charts – they need a mindset 
lens to pick the managers who played to win 
through the downturn and treated their fund like 
a product to continuously improve.
15
As we look toward 2026, the venture and startup 
ecosystem will be operating in a far more complex 
geopolitical and macroeconomic environment 
than the one many funds were built for. 
Fragmentation, trade tensions and industrial 
policy shifts are no longer tail risks; they are the 
baseline. That reality demands a more grounded, 
strategy-driven approach to venture investing.  
From our perspective, this is precisely why 
industrial decarbonization remains not only 
relevant, but essential. The next phase of climate 
innovation will be driven less by regulation or 
ideology, and much more by competitiveness. 
Energy e fficiency, advanced materials, 
electriﬁ cation, digitalization of industrial 
processes and resilient infrastructure are no 
longer “climate bets” — they are productivity bets. 
Companies that reduce emissions by lowering 
costs, improving reliability or strengthening 
supply chains will outperform regardless of 
political cycles. 
“ “
Our investment focus is early-growth (post-
validation, pre-scale), backing deep-tech 
companies at the intersection of industry, energy 
and manufacturing, primarily in Southern

The Unicorn Overhang: Still Private Unicorns By

Unicorn Performance 
As noted in the last slide, the current unicorn formation rate has stabilized at around 10 per month—a far cry from the 2021 peak when nearly 60 unicorns were 
being minted monthly. While the pace has normalized, a deeper issue looms in the form of a “unicorn overhang.” Many of these private unicorns—especially 
those that joined the board over the last decade—still haven’t exited. In fact, less than half of the unicorns founded in the past 15 years have achieved a liquidity 
event.  
This backlog is creating a bottleneck in the venture ecosystem, tying up capital and limiting room for new breakouts. One of the key reasons for this overhang is 
the elevated bar for exits. Today, public markets and strategic acquirers are demanding stronger KPIs—higher revenue, durable growth, and clear paths to 
profitability. As a result, only around 25% of existing unicorns are realistically IPO-ready. The rest fall short—whether due to modest scale, slow growth, or weak 
margins. This growing disconnect between private valuation and public market readiness poses a structural challenge. Until a larger portion of this overhang clears, 
it will likely continue to cast a shadow over late-stage fundraising and exit dynamics.

Secondaries comes with discounts as seen in the charts below. But now, both NewView Capital and StepStone Group are reshaping the narrative around venture 
secondaries, urging investors to move beyond the traditional obsession with discounts. NewView challenges the reliance on last-round markdowns, arguing that 
such benchmarks are often misleading for startups with complex capital structures and volatile growth trajectories. Instead, they advocate for evaluating companies 
based on intrinsic value, growth-adjusted entry multiples, and long-term business fundamentals.  StepStone reinforces this perspective with data showing that deep 
discounts—particularly those exceeding 15%—don’t inherently translate to stronger returns. In fact, pursuing underperforming assets at bargain prices often leads 
to disappointing outcomes. Their findings emphasize that asset quality, not price, is the primary driver of long-term performance. Concentrated investments in high-
conviction, top-tier companies—even at modest premiums—consistently outperform broad portfolios filled with discounted but lower-quality holdings. Together, 
these views reflect a strategic shift: in venture secondaries, disciplined underwriting and selectivity are far more valuable than chasing optical value. The emerging 
consensus is clear—success lies in backing the best companies, not the cheapest ones.

Acquihires, Reverse Acquihires, and Blitzhires 
The reverse acquihire — where Big Tech licenses a startup’s technology and hires away its key talent without acquiring the company — has become a new strategic 
norm in the AI boom. It allows giants like Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon to capture scarce AI expertise while sidestepping antitrust scrutiny tied to 
traditional acquisitions. For Big Tech, these deals accelerate innovation and talent acquisition without regulatory hurdles. For startups, they often bring short-term 
liquidity but long-term disruption — stripping away founders, leadership, and strategic direction while leaving behind “ghost ships” to rebuild.

Strategic implications: 
• Reverse acquihires help Big Tech win the AI talent war and navigate

• For startups and VCs, they represent partial survival but limited upside,

Windsurf Saga 
The Windsurf saga unfolded as a high-stakes drama emblematic of today’s AI talent wars. It began with a near-$3 billion acquisition deal by OpenAI, which 
collapsed suddenly after Microsoft—concerned about intellectual property risks—intervened to block it. Within hours, Windsurf’s CEO and key team members 
were quietly recruited by Google DeepMind through a $2.4 billion "reverse acquihire," focused solely on talent rather than product. This move left the remaining 
250-person team in shock. Over an emotional weekend, interim CEO Jeff Wang worked rapidly to secure a lifeline, culminating in a deal with AI startup Cognition. 
Unlike the Google deal, Cognition’s offer valued the product, IP, and entire team—ensuring continuity and fair treatment of all employees. By Monday, a formal 
acquisition was announced, stabilizing the company and allowing it to continue operating independently.  
The episode triggered widespread commentary across the venture and tech ecosystem, with many criticizing the trend of acquihires that disproportionately reward 
founders while leaving broader teams behind. Strategically, the saga reinforced a new M&A playbook in AI: fast, regulatory-safe deals that prioritize top talent and 
product synergies over conventional acquisitions. In just 72 hours, Windsurf went from collapse to recovery—marking a turning point in how power, people, and 
product are negotiated in the AI era. 
But I’d tread carefully here. There’s a lot of noise circulating on social media—much of it negative toward the founders—but without knowing the full background, 
it’s hard to judge fairly. In fact, based on Garry Tan’s post, situation might not be as dire as some are suggesting. Time will ultimately reveal what really happened.

Venture Fundraising Data – Nuances 
When the top 30 VC firms alone account for nearly 74% of total fundraising, while emerging managers capture just 11%, it’s a clear sign of the times. This "flight 
to familiarity" reflects a deeply risk-off environment, where LPs are leaning heavily on brand-name firms with long track records, and sidelining newer entrants—
even if they bring differentiated strategies. And this concentration is unlikely to shift in H2, as caution continues to outweigh experimentation.  
A key nuance emerging in the current fundraising landscape is the rise of mid-sized funds. Contrary to the popular narrative of a polarized, two-sided market, 
funds in the $100–250 million range have steadily increased their share of total funds (#) in the market since 2023. This middle tier is gaining ground as LPs look 
for specialized strategies with scalable potential—offering a balance between boutique agility and institutional credibility. It's a sign that the venture ecosystem is 
not just consolidating at the top, but also evolving with a more robust middle layer. 
Meanwhile, Europe tells a parallel but distinct story. Private funds there are raising secondaries at a remarkable pace, including within the VC segment. Alongside 
that, debt is playing a larger role. Altogether, these trends paint a picture of an ecosystem still operating under a risk-managed mindset—concentrated capital, 
fewer new bets, and increasing interest in liquidity and defensiveness over bold, early-stage exposure. The appetite for innovation is there—but it’s being routed 
through safer, more predictable vehicles for now.

Venture Performance Data | 1 
A recent PitchBook analysis modeled how venture capital (VC) exposure affects portfolio performance, and the results were mixed. While allocators often look to 
VC for high-growth, innovation-driven returns, capturing those gains has been difficult. From 2000 to 2024, adding VC exposure to a diversified public portfolio 
actually reduced performance, with an annualized excess return of -1.21%. The tradeoff was poor: adjusted volatility hit 16.12% versus 11.43% for the benchmark, 
meaning more risk for weaker returns. Outcomes varied widely, emphasizing how critical manager selection is—strong managers can drive outperformance, while 
weaker ones drag results down. Important point to note is that the PitchBook’s dataset also underrepresents top-performing VC firms, skewing simulations toward 
smaller funds with less access to quality deal flow. This gap likely explains much of the underperformance compared with the Nasdaq 100. 
On a quarterly basis, short-term results were encouraging across private markets in early 2025. MSCI data showed that venture capital and other private market 
strategies posted positive returns in the first quarter. According to the latest update from the MSCI Private Capital Universe, all major segments — private credit,

Venture Performance Data | 2 
Is there performance persistence in Venture? In public markets, it’s well established that alpha doesn’t stick around for long — the managers who beat the market 
one year often fall back to average the next. Private markets, however, play by a different set of rules. They’re less liquid, more opaque, and heavily reliant on 
access to deals and strong execution. Here, “persistence” refers to how much a general partner’s past fund performance can actually predict their future success. 
U.S. Venture Perfomance: The Nasdaq Composite has outperformed Cambridge Associates’ U.S. Venture Capital Index — which tracks over 2,600 VC funds — 
across every time frame: 1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, and even 25 years. And that’s based on average returns, which are skewed upward by a few big winners; the median 
fund likely fares worse. While VC returns should be judged over longer horizons, the data still shows that, on average, investors would have done better simply 
holding a Nasdaq ETF. The takeaway? Treat VC with realistic expectations. It can produce exceptional results, but most funds fall short of their 3–5x targets. Unless 
you have access to top-tier managers or prefer the thrill of the game, you’re probably better off owning the Nasdaq.

250
Venture Diversification, Dispersion, Volatility, and Drawdowns 
1st chart is from Steve Kim’s recent post highlights diversification aspect in Venture. VC investors face two kinds of ruin — mathematical (losing all capital) and 
psychological (giving up too early). The latter is more common and more damaging. Diversification isn’t just about reducing risk; it keeps investors in the game 
long enough to benefit from long-term power-law returns. Power laws define venture outcomes: a few massive winners drive most returns. Concentration risks 
missing those rare outliers, while diversification increases the odds of capturing them — even if individual wins are diluted. In essence, diversification protects 
against both types of ruin: it prevents total loss and provides enough small wins to sustain conviction until the big winners appear. It’s not a defensive tactic; it’s a 
strategy for compounding and surviving long enough to capture asymmetric upside. 
The other two charts highlight the well-known reality that venture capital shows far greater performance dispersion than any other asset class.

264
All About SPVs 
Back in 2024, SPVs were a hot topic. Now, SPVs drew significant attention in Q3, especially after major AI players like OpenAI and Anthropic began tightening 
restrictions on their use. These moves highlight growing concerns around opaque SPV structures and the resale of pre-IPO shares through informal or inflated 
channels. SPVs themselves aren’t the problem—it’s how they’re used. These vehicles have long been a legitimate tool for raising capital to invest in specific deals, 
but a wave of unregulated managers has recently exploited investor hype around pre-IPO opportunities in AI, crypto, and other hot sectors. The real risk lies in 
poor oversight and complex, multi-layered SPV structures that hide excessive fees or unclear ownership. Investors should focus less on the SPV label and more on 
who’s managing it, how it’s structured, and whether proper documentation and transparency are in place. In short, SPVs can be effective for pre-IPO access—but 
only with disciplined due diligence.

265
Fund Structures 
Venture capital is fast becoming a hotbed of fund structuring experimentation—from evergreen vehicles and retail-friendly fund models, to AI roll-up strategies, 
continuation funds, and even tokenization efforts. While some of these approaches are branded as "innovations," many are actually adaptations of long-standing 
structures from other asset classes, now being tailored to fit the unique needs of venture. 
Take evergreen funds—common in private wealth and infrastructure, but now gaining renewed interest in venture for their flexibility and long-term horizon. AI roll-
up funds, a more recent development, have only started gaining traction in the past 12 months. Meanwhile, tokenization efforts like Robinhood’s private stock 
tokens still face regulatory scrutiny and limited traction, though the underlying ambition is clear. 
At the heart of all this movement is a broader trend: the democratization of venture capital. More participants, bigger capital pools, and better access mechanisms 
are being designed—not just for institutional investors, but increasingly for individuals as well. The path is long and complex, but the direction is unmistakable: 
venture is evolving from an elite, gated asset class into a more open, diversified, and inventive ecosystem.

266
Tariffs and LPs 
Most LPs have understandably adopted a risk-off posture, driven largely by broader macroeconomic uncertainty. In turbulent environments, their expectations for 
the venture ecosystem take a backseat to larger portfolio dynamics. Since venture typically represents a relatively small slice of their overall allocation, LPs’ 
decisions are often swayed more by movements in major asset classes like public equities. As a result, shifts in public market’s sentiment can significantly influence 
their willingness to commit to high-risk, long-duration investments like venture capital.

267
Venture M&A 
The venture capital landscape is undergoing a strategic transformation, marked by the blurring of lines between traditional VC, private equity, and corporate 
innovation models. This evolution is driven by a convergence of capital concentration, rising deal sizes, and the need for differentiated value creation beyond just 
capital. On one front, VC firms are increasingly acting like PE players—prioritizing financial discipline, deeper operational involvement, and even strategic 
acquisitions. Acquisitions by traditional VC firms are on pace for an all-time high in 2025, signaling the rise of the "full-stack investor." Firms like Lightspeed, 
a16z, Sequoia, Thrive, and General Catalyst are retooling their structures—Lightspeed notably becoming an RIA—to actively manage portfolio companies and 
unlock broader paths to liquidity. This reflects a clear shift away from the passive "invest and wait" model, toward a more integrated, hands-on approach akin to 
private equity. 
At the same time, tech giants like Meta are also adopting venture-like strategies, acquiring minority stakes in top AI-focused funds (e.g., NFDG) and executing 
targeted acqui-hires—such as bringing in Daniel Gross to lead its new Superintelligence Lab. These moves signal a new era of strategic capital deployment, where 
corporate investors are embedding themselves deeper into early innovation ecosystems to secure both talent and deal flow. Together, these trends underscore a 
new reality: venture is no longer just about high-risk capital—it’s about control, access, and value creation across the full lifecycle of a startup. Whether through PE-
inspired fund models or Big Tech’s venture incursions, the next phase of venture will be defined by more active ownership, structural agility, and cross-model 
convergence.

268
Regulatory News 
In the U.S., the SEC is making a strategic shift toward expanding retail access to private markets by revisiting longstanding constraints on private fund participation 
and modernizing the accredited investor framework. Recent regulatory updates, including relaxed rules on general solicitation under Rule 506(c) enhance the 
capital formation flexibility. While these changes could democratize investment opportunities, wealth advisors urge caution, emphasizing the importance of strong 
regulatory guardrails to protect less experienced investors. Together, these moves reflect a broader policy push to rebalance capital market access while preserving 
investor safeguards.

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognised for temporary differences at the tax rates expected to be applied when the assets are recovered or liabilities are settled, based on those tax rates that are enacted or substantively enacted, except for: ●  When the deferred income tax asset or liability arises from the initial recognition of goodwill or an asset or liability in a transaction that is not a business combination and that, at the time of the transaction, affects neither the accounting nor taxable profits; or ●  When the taxable temporary difference is associated with interests in subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, and the timing of the reversal can be controlled and it is probable that the temporary difference will not reverse in the foreseeable future.   Deferred tax assets are recognised for deductible temporary differences and unused tax losses only if it is probable that future taxable amounts will be available to utilise those temporary differences and losses.   The carrying amount of recognised and unrecognised deferred tax assets are reviewed at each reporting date. Deferred tax assets recognised are reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that future taxable profits will be available for the carrying amount to be recovered. Previously unrecognised deferred tax assets are recognised to the extent that it is probable that there are future taxable profits available to recover the asset.   Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only where there is a legally enforceable right to offset current tax assets against current tax liabilities and deferred tax assets against deferred tax liabilities; and they relate to the same taxable authority on either the same taxable entity or different taxable entities which intend to settle simultaneously.   (i) Current and non-current classification Assets and liabilities are presented in the statement of financial position based on current and non-current classification. All other assets are classified as non-current.   A liability is classified as current when: it is either expected to be settled in the consolidated entity's normal operating cycle; it is held primarily for the purpose of trading; it is due to be settled within 12 months after the reporting period; or there is no unconditional right to defer the settlement of the liability for at least 12 months after the reporting period. All other liabilities are classified as non-current.   Deferred tax assets and liabilities are always classified as non-current. Net realisable value is the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less the estimated costs of completion and the estimated costs necessary to make the sale.   Associates Associates are entities over which the consolidated entity has significant influence but not control or joint control. Investments in associates are accounted for using the equity method. Under the equity method, the share of the profits or losses of the associate is recognised in profit or loss and the share of the movements in equity is recognised in other comprehensive income. Investments in associates are carried in the statement of financial position at cost plus post-acquisition changes in the consolidated entity's share of net assets of the associate. Goodwill relating to the associate is included in the carrying amount of the investment and is neither amortised nor individually tested for impairment. The consolidated entity discontinues the use of the equity method upon the loss of significant influence over the associate and recognises any retained investment at its fair value. Any difference between the associate's carrying amount, fair value of the retained investment and proceeds from disposal is recognised in profit or loss. The measurement of the loss allowance depends upon the consolidated entity's assessment at the end of each reporting period as to whether the financial instrument's credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition, based on reasonable and supportable information that is available, without undue cost or effort to obtain.   Where there has not been a significant increase in exposure to credit risk since initial recognition, a 12-month expected credit loss allowance is estimated. This represents a portion of the asset's lifetime expected credit losses that is attributable to a default event that is possible within the next 12 months. Where a financial asset has become credit impaired or where it is determined that credit risk has increased significantly, the loss allowance is based on the asset's lifetime expected credit losses. The amount of expected credit loss recognised is measured on the basis of the probability weighted present value of anticipated cash shortfalls over the life of the instrument discounted at the original effective interest rate.   For financial assets mandatorily measured at fair value through other comprehensive income, the loss allowance is recognised in other comprehensive income with a corresponding expense through profit or loss. Founder Newsletter #40
Feb 12, 2025
1

In today's newsletter:
Seattle Founder Day coming up on March 26th! Join us for a full day of learning, networking and inspiration!
Fireside Chat: our next insightful investor forum with Jenny Fielding from Everything VC on March 12th.
Founder programs, resources, grants and accelerators you should know
Our Latest Funding Report: Check out the startups that got funded this month
We are on Slack: If you haven't already, join our exclusive G&W Slack channel here!
ICYMI: watch our previous fireside chat with Sydney Paige Thomas from Symphonic Capital here.
Upcoming
In Person: Seattle Founders, we are back with Founder Day!
Graham & Walker is thrilled to bring their most impactful program for women founders to Seattle! Founder Day is a day of high-impact, high-substance programming designed to help early-stage founders meaningfully move their businesses forward.
Select founders will be invited to participate in office hours, where they’ll meet 1-1 with an outstanding slate of mentors – investors, legal experts, and more.
Following Founder Day, you are invited to join us for a panel and reception to meet, mingle and connect with other founders.
Limited seats only. Apply here.
Virtual: Join us for an inspiring fireside chat with Jenny Fielding from Everywhere Ventures!
Jenny Fielding is one of the most active pre-seed investors globally, having backed 300+ companies as the first check in. As the co-founder and Managing Partner of Everywhere Ventures, she has built a powerhouse community of 500+ founders and operators investing in the future of money, health, and work.
Before launching her own fund, Jenny spent 7.5 years at Techstars, where she helped shape a portfolio now valued at over $10B. She’s also a 2x founder, a trained lawyer, and an adjunct professor at Columbia University and Cornell Tech.
🔥 Don’t miss this deep dive into early-stage investing, founder communities, and what it takes to build in today’s market.
March 12th, 11a PT/ 2p ET 📍 RSVP here.
Founder Resources
Accelerators & Programs
G&W’s Founder Day happening in person in Seattle on March 26th. Join us for a day full of learning, connection and inspiration at Seattle brand new hub for founders: Seattle Foundations.
Future Builders Fellowship (2025): This program supports US founders to tackle various social issues through training, resources, and residencies in Washington, DC, and Atlanta. Apply here by 2/16.
Climate Fellowship (2025): This program brings together entrepreneurs to address climate issues. It provides training, resources, and an 8-week residency in Washington, DC. Apply here by 2/16.
Wells Fargo Equitable Access Boost Camp is now accepting applications for an exclusive 12-week accelerator program. Learn more and apply by 2/21.
Y Combinator Spring 2025: Y Combinator is accepting applications for its Spring 2025 Batch (April–June in San Francisco). Apply by February 11 at 8 PM PT for a decision by 3/12
Grants
Boundless Futures Foundation’s grants to businesses are awarded directly to female entrepreneurs who put social impact front and center in their business products or practices. Learn more and apply here by 2/15.
Main Street Ventures’ funding programs support local entrepreneurs in the idea/prototype and revenue stages with equity free business funding. Learn more and apply here by 2/16.
Lenovo Evolve Small AI Grant: Applications are now open. Small businesses can apply here by 2/17.
In celebration of Black History Month, Citi Trends is acknowledging Black entrepreneurs that are making history in their community today. Calling all the best & brightest Black changemakers to apply here by 2/28.
What we are reading
This article from First Round Review outlining How to Nail Founder-Led Sales is full of fantastic tactics from founders and growth experts who have gone from $0-$5M.
Duolingo’s handbook: how this successful company was built while sustaining it’s quirky culture
Resources
WA based Founders: Our friends at WTIA offer competitive, cost-effective health plans that grow with your business. With access to 27 plan options, and a wide range of wellness programs, you can provide your employees with comprehensive coverage while simplifying your admin. Join over 400 companies leveraging WTIA's purchasing power to offer benefits that make a difference—like $0 cost virtual visits and wellness incentives like a free Apple Watch. Reach out to get a quote.
More Cloud Credits! Founders in our community are now eligible for even more Cloud credits thanks to our partnership with AWS Activate program. Build, experiment, and scale with up to $25k in AWS Activate cloud credits. Apply here and use our unique and org id 8ipK4. Only FFA founders are eligible for these benefits.
G&W Benefits
Find our latest and greatest G&W Founder Benefits here to get your hands on the exclusive partner perks available to our founder community!
Funding Report
Hinge Bio, a privately-held biotechnology company, announced the closing of a $30M Series A’ financing led by Point72. Joining Point72 are Ridgeback Capital, InVivium Capital, and Lightswitch Capital, and others.
Hone Health, a leading telehealth clinic specializing in preventative and proactive longevity care, announced that it completed a $33M Series A funding round with participation by Tribe Capital, PIF, Republic Capital, Vibe VC, Humbition, Hanwha, Gaingels, Looking Glass Capital, FJ Labs, and Agent Capital.
Delfina Care Inc. (Delfina), a healthcare technology company solving the maternal health crisis with an AI-powered care system, announced the successful close of its $17M Series A funding round led by U.S. Venture Partners (USVP) including participation from new investors ARTIS Ventures, Mayo Clinic, and Tokio Marine Future Fund. Delfina’s existing investors also participated in the round, including Story Ventures, SemperVirens, Bread and Butter Ventures, Boutique Ventures, and Chelsea Clinton’s Metrodora Ventures.
(…Continue reading the Funding Report on the blog)
ICYMI
Catch up on February’s fireside chat with Sydney Paige Thomas where she shares her journey that led to starting Symphonic Capital, her passion for their thesis and why she believes one can be a successful VC fund that also creates lasting impact.
Graham & Walker does two things: we support founders & we invest in founders. Wherever you are, we are here for you.
We invest in deeply human problems, especially in the areas of health, work and caretaking. If you’re an early stage woman-founded tech company in North America ready to change the world, we want to meet you.
Pitch the Fund
Join our Slack to share resources and connect with other female and nonbinary founders!

Venture Everywhere, Pre-Seed, and Why Venture Doesn't Scale with Jenny Fielding
top of page
Jenny Fielding is a Cofounder and General Partner of Everywhere Ventures. Jenny is a pre-seed investor with a fascinating background. She’s a founder, lawyer by training, has lived in 12 countries, and ran Techstars New York for many years. She’s also the author of Venture Everywhere, a book which comes out in March. We talked about Jenny’s strategy, why venture doesn’t scale, why everywhere doesn't use follow-on capital in its funds, and how Everywhere is navigating the Seed and AI markets.
The episode is now available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Amazon, and YouTube Music.
Chapters
00:00 Introduction to Jenny Fielding and Everywhere Ventures
02:59 The Philosophy of Everywhere Ventures
06:07 Understanding Pre-Seed Investments
09:02 The Role of Community in Venture Capital
12:04 Navigating the Seed Market Today
15:01 The Impact of AI on Valuations
18:01 The Importance of Global Mindset
20:58 Challenges in Scaling Communities
24:01 Final Thoughts and Book Release
Takeaways
Innovation is everywhere, and geography is becoming less important.
Pre-seed investment is crucial for helping companies find product-market fit.
Building a strong community of founders and operators enhances deal flow.
Communities take time to build and require trust and intimacy.
The seed market has become more challenging, with higher expectations for metrics.
AI valuations are rising, but we focus on the people behind the companies.
A global mindset is essential for entrepreneurs in today's world.
The venture capital landscape is evolving, with more capital available at early stages.
Scaling a venture firm doesn't always mean increasing fund size; quality matters more.
Jenny's book 'Venture Everywhere' highlights diverse entrepreneurial stories from around the world.

About - Everywhere with Jenny
Everywhere with Jenny

Home
Podcast
About
Hi, I’m Jenny!
Subscribe
After attending law school and working in finance, I found myself falling in love with technology - first as a founder of two mobile companies and now as an early stage investor. Being a founder was the most humbling and challenging work of my life, and I’ve channeled many of the learnings into my investment style.
I was the Managing Director at Techstars for 7.5 years where I led investments into companies that now have a market cap of over $10B, prior to co-founding the global venture capital firm, Everywhere Ventures (formerly The Fund.) Across these entities, I’ve been the first-money into 300+ tech-enabled companies and have worked with hundreds of founders at the zero to one phase.
When I’m not investing, you can find me catching up with founders around the world or hanging out with my students at Columbia University and Cornell Tech where I’m an Adjunct Professor.
